front: How many SQE2 assessments are there, and how are they split between oral and written?
back: There are 16 assessments in total: 4 oral and 12 written. The 4 oral assessments are taken over two half days and the 12 written assessments over three half days, five half days in all.

front: Does SQE2 contain any multiple choice questions?
back: No. Every one of the 16 SQE2 assessments is performance based. There are no multiple choice questions anywhere in SQE2. Any material describing SQE2 as a multiple choice exam is describing something else, usually SQE1.

front: Name the six legal skills assessed in SQE2 and say which are oral.
back: Client interview with attendance note or legal analysis, and advocacy, are assessed orally. Case and matter analysis, legal research, legal writing and legal drafting are assessed in writing.

front: Is there a separate negotiation assessment in SQE2?
back: No. There is no separate negotiation assessment, but every delivery of SQE2 contains at least one assessment involving negotiation. It can appear in the client interview and attendance note, in case and matter analysis, or in legal writing.

front: In which three skills does negotiation never appear?
back: Negotiation never appears in advocacy, legal research or legal drafting. It is also never labelled as a negotiation exercise when it does appear, so you must recognise it yourself.

front: List the five SQE2 practice areas with their underlying black letter law.
back: Criminal Law and Practice, underpinned by criminal liability; Dispute Resolution, underpinned by contract law and tort; Property Practice, underpinned by land law; Wills and the Administration of Estates, underpinned by trusts law; and Business Law and Practice, underpinned by contract law.

front: Which practice areas carry money laundering, and which carries financial services?
back: Money laundering is examinable in both Business Law and Practice and Property Practice. Financial services is examinable only in Business Law and Practice.

front: State the timings for the client interview station.
back: You get 10 minutes to read the instructing email and the accompanying documents, then 25 minutes to conduct the interview. The reading period covers both the email and the documents, so a leisurely reading method will fail.

front: How long is the attendance note station and how is it produced?
back: The attendance note and legal analysis station is 25 minutes and is written by hand. It is the only handwritten element of SQE2.

front: State the two timings for the advocacy station.
back: You get 45 minutes of preparation, then 15 minutes of submissions to a judge.

front: Give the timings for the four written skills.
back: Case and matter analysis is 60 minutes, legal research is 60 minutes, legal writing is 30 minutes and legal drafting is 45 minutes. Legal writing is the shortest of the four written skills assessments, although the 25 minute handwritten attendance note is shorter still.

front: What is the fixed oral pairing on Oral Day 1?
back: FRONT: Which practice areas carry advocacy, and which carry the client interview? BACK: Advocacy is assessed only in Dispute Resolution and in Criminal Law and Practice. The client interview with attendance note is assessed only in Property Practice and in Wills and the Administration of Estates. Each oral half day carries one advocacy assessment and one interview, but the specification does not fix which pairing falls on which half day.

front: What is the fixed oral pairing on Oral Day 2?
back: FRONT: Where is advocacy never assessed, and where is the client interview never assessed? BACK: Advocacy is never assessed in Property Practice, in Wills and the Administration of Estates, or in Business Law and Practice. The client interview is never assessed in Dispute Resolution, in Criminal Law and Practice, or in Business Law and Practice. Business Law and Practice has no oral station at all.

front: State the negative version of the oral pairing: where do advocacy and interview never appear?
back: Advocacy is never assessed in Property Practice, Wills and the Administration of Estates, or Business Law and Practice. The client interview is never assessed in Dispute Resolution, Criminal Law and Practice, or Business Law and Practice.

front: Which practice area has no oral station at all?
back: Business Law and Practice has no oral station. It is assessed only in writing, but it occupies the whole of written Day 3.

front: Set out the fixed written pattern across the three written half days.
back: Written Day 1 is two exercises in Dispute Resolution and two in Criminal Law and Practice. Written Day 2 is two in Property Practice and two in Wills and the Administration of Estates. Written Day 3 is all four written skills in Business Law and Practice.

front: Why is it wrong to treat Business Law and Practice as a small subject because it has no oral station?
back: Business Law and Practice takes the whole of written Day 3, so it carries four written exercises against two for each other practice area. It is the largest single written commitment in SQE2, and treating it as small gets the weighting exactly backwards.

front: How is each individual assessment criterion graded?
back: Each criterion is graded on a scale from A to F by a trained assessor making a global professional judgment. The assessor forms an overall view of your performance on that criterion rather than adding up points against a checklist.

front: Convert the SQE2 grades A to F into marks and state what each means.
back: A is 5 marks for superior performance well above the competency requirements, B is 4 for a clearly satisfactory performance that clearly meets them, and C is 3 for a marginal pass that on balance just meets them. D is 2 for a marginal fail, E is 1 for a clearly unsatisfactory performance, and F is 0 for poor performance well below the requirements.

front: What separates a C from a B in practice?
back: The gap between a marginal pass and a clearly satisfactory performance is usually made of ordinary professional habits rather than brilliance: answering the question actually asked, addressing the client rather than the examiner, and dealing with the awkward point instead of avoiding it.

front: Can a strong grade on one criterion rescue a weak grade on another within the same assessment?
back: No. Every criterion is graded independently. Clear, well structured writing does not compensate for law applied incorrectly, and correct law does not compensate for advice the client could not follow.

front: How are skills and application of law weighted across SQE2 as a whole?
back: They are weighted equally. Half the available credit is for how well you work as a solicitor and half is for how well you apply the law. Candidates arriving from SQE1 tend to over invest in the law half.

front: Who marks the client interview, and on what criteria?
back: The client interview is marked by the assessor who plays the client, and it is marked on skills only. There are no application of law criteria for the interview itself.

front: Who marks the attendance note, advocacy and the written stations, and on what?
back: A solicitor marks them, on both skills and application of law. So the interview and attendance note form a single station assessed by two different people against two different sets of criteria, and the law you spot in the interview room earns its marks only in the attendance note.

front: How does the SQE2 pass mark work?
back: There is one overall pass mark for SQE2 as a whole, with no separate oral or written pass mark and no requirement to pass each station individually. Performance is aggregated across all 16 assessments and the pass mark is scaled at each sitting under the SRA Marking and Standard Setting Policy, so no fixed percentage exists.

front: Which three SQE1 areas are not assessed at SQE2 at all?
back: The Legal System of England and Wales, including constitutional, administrative and EU law; Legal Services, except money laundering and financial services; and Solicitors' Accounts.

front: What is the SQE2 law cut off date?
back: The law examined is the law as it stood four calendar months before the first assessment in the assessment window. Anything in force after that date is outside the assessment, and you are not tested on the development of the law.

front: Describe the SQE2 assessment conditions for the written stations.
back: The written assessments are computer based on the Pearson VUE platform. There is no spell check, and a highlighter is available only on that platform, so practise with it. No books or notes may be brought in and nothing is open book.

front: What level of legal detail is expected, and how are rates and thresholds handled?
back: SQE2 tests fundamental legal principles at the standard of a newly qualified solicitor who can look detail up later. For every station except legal research you are given the materials you would look up. In tax questions the monetary values, rates and thresholds are given to you; what you must bring is knowledge that a relief or exemption exists and its conditions.

front: When must you cite specific cases or statutory authorities in SQE2?
back: Only in legal research, where citing specific cases and statutory or regulatory authorities is part of the skill assessed, and where a case name or provision is simply the normal professional term for the rule, such as Rylands v Fletcher, CPR Part 36 or a section 25 notice. Elsewhere, apply the principle rather than reciting its source.

front: Why should the interview and the attendance note be treated as two assessments rather than one?
back: They are two halves of one station, but they are marked separately, by different people, against different criteria. You can perform beautifully in the room and still fail the paper, so each half needs its own preparation.

front: In which two practice areas is the client interview assessed, and on which oral day?
back: Oral day 1 is the interview in Property Practice. Oral day 2 is the interview in Wills and the Administration of Estates. It is never assessed in Dispute Resolution, Criminal Law and Practice or Business Law and Practice.

front: What sort of scenarios should you practise interviewing on, and which should you avoid?
back: Practise on property and wills problems: a purchase with a title problem, a client adding a partner to the deeds, a bereaved sibling working out who inherits, an executor facing an unhelpful bank. Do not practise on personal injury or a client charged with an offence, because those are advocacy problems.

front: What are the four things you should produce during the 10 minute reading period?
back: The client's name and how they connect to everyone else mentioned; three or four headings for the areas the partner's email requires you to cover; the gaps only the client can fill, written as questions; and anything that already smells like a conduct problem. Not a full script.

front: How should you use the 10 minutes of reading time across the email and the documents?
back: Read the partner's email twice and everything else once. The email is your instructions: it tells you who is coming in, what the firm already knows and often what the partner wants covered.

front: State the five skills criteria for the client interview.
back: Listen and question effectively so the client can tell you what is important to them; communicate and explain in a way suitable for that client to understand; conduct yourself professionally and treat the client with courtesy, respect and politeness, including respecting diversity where relevant; demonstrate client focus in your approach to the client and the issues; and establish and maintain an effective relationship so as to build trust and confidence.

front: What earns no marks at all in the interview half of the station?
back: Reciting section numbers and producing a complete answer to the legal problem earn nothing, because the interview has no application of law criteria. The lay client in the room is grading you on whether they left feeling heard, understood and looked after.

front: How much advice should you give in the interview room?
back: Enough preliminary advice to reassure the client that you have understood the problem, that the firm deals with it regularly and that there is a route through it. You are not expected to give detailed advice; detailed legal analysis belongs in the attendance note, which is where the law is marked.

front: What is wrong with telling the client for 25 minutes that you will take instructions and write to them?
back: It leaves the client without trust or confidence in you, and trust and confidence is an express criterion. Preliminary advice should be confident and honest, commit to nothing that might be wrong, and name the next step.

front: Set out the repeatable five stage core of the interview and the time each takes.
back: FRONT: Set out the repeatable interview structure and the time each stage takes. BACK: Greeting and introductions about one minute, purpose and outline about one minute, listening phase about eight minutes, funnelling to closed questions about eight minutes, summarising back about three minutes, preliminary advice and next steps about three minutes, costs and client care where relevant about one minute, and closing in under a minute.

front: What belongs in the purpose and outline stage of the interview?
back: Tell the client what will happen so nothing surprises them: that you will listen first, then ask detailed questions, then summarise back for correction, then agree next steps. Confirm that everything they tell you is confidential to the firm and check they are content to proceed.

front: How should the listening phase be conducted?
back: Open with one broad invitation such as asking the client to say in their own words what has brought them in, then let them talk. Use minimal encouragers, do not interrupt to correct a legal misdescription and do not start advising. Keep notes short and keep looking up, because a head down for eight minutes loses the relationship criteria.

front: What is the funnelling phase for, and what sort of questions does it use?
back: It works through your headings and fills the gaps, using closed questions for hard facts such as dates, names, amounts and whether anything has been signed. Probe a thin answer with a request to tell you more, and signpost each move to a new topic.

front: Why does summarising back earn its three minutes?
back: Repeating the instructions in compressed form and inviting correction repairs your mishearings and prompts the client to volunteer the thing they held back. Close it with a direct question asking whether you have missed anything.

front: What makes a next steps section in the interview strong rather than vague?
back: Concrete steps with owners and timescales: what you will do and by when, what the client must send and by when, and when you will next be in touch. Naming who does what is the difference between a promise and a plan.

front: How do you deal with costs in the interview?
back: If the partner's email tells you to deal with costs, cover the basis of the charge, an estimate or range, VAT and disbursements, and a client care letter to follow setting out the complaints procedure. If costs are not in your instructions, one sentence promising a written estimate is enough.

front: How should you respond when a client becomes upset during the interview?
back: Stop asking questions and acknowledge it, telling the client to take their time. Offer a pause or a break and do not talk over the silence. Return to the painful topic later and warn the client before you do.

front: How should you check that a client has understood your explanation?
back: Ask the client to tell you their understanding in their own words. Asking whether something makes sense almost always gets a yes, so it proves nothing.

front: What does respecting diversity require in practice in the interview?
back: It is an express criterion, so adjust your communication to the client rather than expecting the reverse: slow down, drop or explain jargon on first use, and offer practical adjustments such as writing key points down, a home visit or an interpreter. Do not guess at names, pronouns or family structures; ask.

front: A relative attending with the client keeps answering for them. What do you do?
back: Treat it as a capacity and independence issue as well as a conduct one. Address it courteously, thanking the third party but explaining that you need to hear the instructions from the client themselves and may need to see the client alone for part of the meeting.

front: The client presses you for a figure or a guarantee. What is the three part reply?
back: Acknowledge the question as reasonable, explain honestly what information you are missing, and commit to when and how you will answer it. A guess is a professional risk and a flat refusal damages the relationship.

front: If the client presses a second time for a number you cannot give, what can you still offer?
back: Hold the line and give the shape of the answer rather than the number, for example that debts are paid before anything is distributed, so what the house sells for is not what the beneficiaries receive.

front: What is the commonest interview failure, and what is the mechanical cure?
back: Talking over the client: interrupting answers, finishing sentences, delivering a speech. It is fatal because four of the five criteria depend on the client having space. After asking a question, close your mouth and count to three, and aim to speak for less than a third of the 25 minutes.

front: Why is confident detailed advice in the first ten minutes dangerous?
back: The client script usually contains a fact that has not emerged yet and that changes the answer. A candidate who announces at minute six that the estate passes on intestacy looks foolish when a will made in Spain appears at minute fourteen. Gather first, advise second, and phrase preliminary advice provisionally.

front: State the three skills criteria for the attendance note.
back: Record all relevant information, identify appropriate next steps, and provide client focused advice.

front: State the three application of law criteria for the attendance note.
back: Apply the law correctly to the client's situation, apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation, and identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.

front: What is the difference between applying the law correctly and applying it comprehensively?
back: Correctly means the law is right and applied to these facts rather than recited. Comprehensively means you cover every legal issue the facts raise, not just the first. Notes most often drop a grade on the second, by writing an excellent paragraph on the first issue and never reaching the second and third.

front: How do you earn the ethics criterion in an attendance note?
back: Name the issue, state your judgment and state the action you will take. Ethics is pervasive and never flagged, so nobody will tell you a conduct point is there, and simply flagging it without resolving it is not enough.

front: How does negotiation typically appear in the interview and attendance note station?
back: Usually as an offer already on the table, such as a buyer's reduced offer after a survey or a sibling proposing to buy out the others. Take instructions on what the client wants and would accept, record those parameters in the note, and advise on the strengths and weaknesses of the client's position rather than simply passing the offer on.

front: What headings should the handwritten attendance note use, and what presentation standard applies?
back: Use headings for purpose of meeting, instructions and information obtained, advice given, legal analysis, ethical and professional conduct issues, and next steps, under a header giving the matter, reference, who attended and the time engaged. Marks are not lost for spelling, grammar or formatting that does not affect legal accuracy, clarity or certainty, so speed and completeness beat elegance.

front: In which practice areas is advocacy assessed, and on which oral days?
back: Oral day 1 is a submission in Dispute Resolution and oral day 2 is a submission in Criminal Law and Practice. Advocacy is never assessed in Property Practice, Wills and the Administration of Estates or Business Law and Practice.

front: Can the advocacy station involve negotiation?
back: No. Negotiation appears only in the client interview and attendance note, case and matter analysis or legal writing. There is no opponent in the advocacy room; you address a judge alone and ask for an order.

front: What must you extract from the partner's email at once in the advocacy station?
back: Who your client is, which court you are appearing in, what application is being made, and which side you act for. Candidates lose marks every sitting by preparing for the wrong side or by addressing a judge at the wrong level.

front: What documents might the advocacy file contain in each practice area?
back: In Dispute Resolution, a claim form and particulars of claim, a defence, a witness statement in support, correspondence and an order of the court. In Criminal Law and Practice, a charge sheet, a police summary, a record of previous convictions, a defence proof of evidence and a pre-sentence report.

front: Who plays and marks the judge in the advocacy station, and on what?
back: A solicitor of England and Wales plays the judge and marks you on both skills and application of law. This differs from the client interview, where the assessor plays the client and marks skills only, so in advocacy both halves of the mark sheet are live before a qualified lawyer who knows the correct answer.

front: What should you conclude if the judge interrupts your submission with questions?
back: Nothing negative. Judicial questions are part of the assessment design and how you handle them bears directly on two of the five skills criteria. An uninterrupted 15 minutes is unusual, so build a submission that survives being interrupted.

front: Why should you not write out a script during the 45 minutes of preparation?
back: A read script destroys eye contact, collapses under the first question and reads as recitation rather than argument. Prepare headings and a short opening instead of full sentences.

front: How should the 45 minutes of advocacy preparation be divided?
back: Five minutes on the email and the court, five minutes identifying the legal test and its limbs, fifteen minutes marshalling the facts limb by limb, ten minutes anticipating the judge, and ten minutes on structure and delivery.

front: Why write out the limbs of the legal test as a numbered list?
back: Almost every advocacy station turns on a test with limbs or stages, and that numbered list becomes the skeleton of your submission. It is also what the marker checks when scoring you on applying the law correctly and comprehensively.

front: What does marshalling the facts limb by limb involve, and why does it matter?
back: Go through the file with the limbs in front of you and place every fact under the limb it serves, noting the document and page. It satisfies the criterion of including all key relevant facts. A submission that states the test correctly and never touches the file is an application of law pass at best and a skills failure.

front: Which three judicial questions should you have answered before you stand up?
back: What is your best point, what is your worst point, and what exactly are you asking me to do.

front: Give the correct mode of address for each level of judge.
back: A District Judge, including a District Judge (Magistrates' Courts), is addressed as Judge. A Circuit Judge is Your Honour. A High Court judge is My Lord or My Lady, referred to as Your Lordship or Your Ladyship. A bench of lay magistrates is addressed through the chair as Sir or Madam, or collectively as Your Worships.

front: In the magistrates' court, to whom do you direct legal submissions?
back: To the bench, not to the legal adviser or court clerk, even when one is present. Stand to address the court and remain standing while you speak.

front: What are the conventions on naming the parties in your submission?
back: Refer to your client by name and title, to the other party by name, and to a defendant in criminal proceedings by surname with an appropriate title. Do not use first names alone, and do not say my client for fifteen minutes when the court would find a name easier to follow.

front: What must a good advocacy opening contain?
back: Who you are, who you act for, the application being made, the shape of what follows, and the order sought. That takes about twenty seconds and scores at once under structure, persuasion and engagement.

front: What is the cheapest way to score on clear and logical structure?
back: Signposting as you go, announcing when one point ends and identifying the next. A listener who cannot see the argument written down follows it only through signposts.

front: What is the correct sequence when the judge intervenes, including on a point you meant to take later?
back: Stop speaking immediately, never talk over the bench, listen to the whole question, and answer it in one or two sentences before developing the point. If it was a later point, answer it now and say so, because saying you will come to it and moving on reads as evasion.

front: What do you say when you do not know the answer to a judicial question?
back: Say so plainly and offer what you can from the material you do have. An honest answer scores. A confident invention is both a skills failure and an ethical failure, because you must never mislead the court.

front: What should you do when the bench has clearly accepted a point?
back: Stop making it. Repetition after the judge has agreed with you wastes minutes from a 15 minute slot and irritates the person marking you.

front: How do you concede a weak point without abandoning your client?
back: Concede the narrow point, then reframe the question for the court onto the ground where you win. Give away only what is genuinely lost. Denying the obvious loses credibility on everything else you say, and conceding everything means you have stopped acting for the client.

front: How does the duty not to mislead the court rank against the client's interests?
back: It is absolute and it outranks the client's interests. If you know of a document, fact or procedural irregularity that must be drawn to the court's attention, draw it, and you cannot assert something you know to be untrue even on instructions.

front: How are ethical issues presented in the advocacy file?
back: They are never flagged. Nothing in the file is labelled as an ethics point; it sits there looking like an ordinary detail, and the marker watches whether you spot it and resolve it honestly and with integrity.

front: How should an advocacy submission close?
back: With the order you want, expressed as an order a judge could actually make, including consequential orders such as costs. Then offer a fallback order if the primary order is refused, and finish by inviting questions and sitting down.

front: Is offering a fallback position a sign of weakness?
back: No. It is what a competent litigator does, and it shows the marker you have thought about what happens if you lose. Prepare the alternative order during your preparation time, not on your feet.

front: State the five skills criteria for advocacy.
back: Use appropriate language and behaviour; adopt a clear and logical structure; present a persuasive argument; interact with and engage the court appropriately; and include all key relevant facts.

front: State the three application of law criteria for advocacy and the consequence of failing one half.
back: Apply the law correctly to the client's situation, apply it comprehensively, and identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity. Skills and application of law are weighted equally, so a polished submission on the wrong legal test fails half the mark sheet and an immaculate but mumbled recitation fails the other half.

front: Set out the order of a bail application.
back: Open and identify the application, state the presumption in favour of bail and the ground of objection, answer each ground in turn with facts from the file such as community ties, settled address, employment, previous compliance and the strength of the evidence, then offer conditions that meet the specific risk raised, and close by asking for bail on those conditions.

front: Set out the order of a plea in mitigation.
back: Open, confirm the plea and the credit due for it, address the offence by culpability and harm and where it sits in the guideline, take the aggravating features head on, then turn to personal mitigation, remorse, employment, health, dependants and progress. If custody is in play, address the effect of immediate custody and why a suspended sentence with requirements would meet the purposes of sentencing, then close with the specific disposal sought.

front: How do you structure a submission for summary judgment, an interim injunction and relief from sanctions?
back: For summary judgment, state the test and apply it to the pleaded defence point by point, dealing expressly with the second limb of no other compelling reason for a trial, which candidates forget. For an injunction, take the court through serious issue to be tried, adequacy of damages for either side and the balance of convenience, offering the cross undertaking in damages unasked. For relief from sanctions, use the three stages: seriousness of the breach, the reason for it stated honestly, and all the circumstances including efficient conduct at proportionate cost and enforcing compliance.

front: Must you cite authorities in the advocacy station?
back: No. You are not required to recall case names or cite statutory or regulatory authorities, except where the name is simply the normal term for the rule or step, such as CPR Part 36, a Part 24 application or a Part 8 claim. State the test accurately in your own words: a correct statement without a citation scores, and a citation attached to a misstated test does not.

front: How long is the case and matter analysis station, and in which practice areas can it appear?
back: It is a written, computer based station of exactly 60 minutes. It is sat three times across the three written half days, so across a full delivery it can appear in Criminal Law and Practice, Dispute Resolution, Property Practice, Wills and the Administration of Estates, and Business Law and Practice.

front: What is the task in case and matter analysis?
back: You are given a covering email or memorandum from a partner plus a bundle of documents, and must produce a written report to the partner setting out a legal analysis of the case and advice for the client. Where the matter involves a dispute or a deal to be settled, the report may also be required to set out options and strategies for negotiation.

front: Should you always include negotiation content in a case and matter analysis report?
back: No. Negotiation content may be required but will not necessarily be, so never assume it is wanted unless the partner's instructions ask for it.

front: What are the two structural failures that cost most of the marks in this station?
back: Reciting the file back to the partner instead of analysing it, and giving a single option instead of comparing options and setting out the consequences of each. Both are structural rather than legal failures.

front: Who is the audience for the report, and what register does that require?
back: The report goes to a partner, who is a solicitor. They do not need the law in lay terms, reassurance or a paragraph thanking them for their instructions. The register is analytical: propositions of law stated plainly, applied to identified facts, with conclusions.

front: If the report is written to a partner, how can it also be client focused?
back: The format is a note to a professional and the content is advice to a person. Client focused advice names the client's commercial or personal objective, weighs the options against it, and says what is recommended and why. Hold both at once.

front: Why must the client's stated aim appear expressly in your analysis?
back: Client focus is a marking criterion, and the client's aim drives the recommendation. A technically excellent report recommending four years of litigation to a client who has said they cannot afford it is not client focused, however well the law is applied.

front: How should the 60 minutes be allocated?
back: Fifteen minutes to read and annotate, five minutes to plan the structure, thirty five minutes to write, and five minutes to check.

front: What should you read first in the 15 minute reading period, and what should you highlight?
back: Read the partner's instructions first, twice, because anything you write outside them earns nothing. Then read the bundle using the platform's highlighter, marking dates, sums of money, names of parties, defined terms in any contract, and anything resembling a deadline or a limitation period.

front: What does the five minute planning step consist of, and what mistake does it prevent?
back: Type your headings into the answer box before writing any prose. It costs almost nothing and prevents the most expensive mistake in this station, which is discovering at minute 52 that you have written three paragraphs on liability and none on remedy.

front: What are you checking for in the final five minutes?
back: There is no spell check, so you check meaning rather than typography: whether the recommendation actually follows from your analysis, whether every option has a consequence attached, whether you have addressed ethics if the papers raised it, and whether the sums and dates match the documents.

front: If you fall behind the clock in case and matter analysis, what do you cut?
back: Cut the length of your analysis of each issue rather than dropping an issue. A short paragraph on limitation earns marks; no paragraph on limitation earns none.

front: What goes in the heading and purpose sections of the report?
back: The heading names the report, the client, the matter, the person it is to and from, and the date, with the file reference. The purpose is one or two sentences saying what the report does and what it does not do, for example excluding an issue on which documents are awaited.

front: What belongs in the summary of key facts, and what does not?
back: Only the facts that carry legal weight, usually four to eight sentences. A fact belongs there if you will rely on it later in the analysis. It is not a chronology of the file, and where a fact is disputed or unknown you say so rather than pretending the file is clearer than it is.

front: Why list the legal issues as numbered one line entries?
back: It gives the partner the shape of the matter in fifteen seconds and gives the assessor a visible map of how comprehensive your identification of the issues has been. List them in the order you will analyse them.

front: What must each issue analysis section contain?
back: State the legal principle, apply it to the identified facts, and reach a conclusion, including how confident you are in it. Say what evidence would strengthen or weaken the position. Draw the inference yourself rather than leaving it to the partner.

front: For each option you set out, what four things must you give?
back: The likely outcome, the cost in money and time, the risk, and the effect on anything the client has said they care about.

front: Give examples of realistic options in a dispute and in a transaction.
back: In a dispute: doing nothing, writing a letter before claim, referring the matter to mediation, making a Part 36 offer, issuing proceedings, or accepting a compromise already on the table. In a transaction: proceeding on the current terms, requiring an indemnity, requiring a price reduction, requiring a deed of variation, or withdrawing.

front: What happens if your report sets out three options but declines to choose one?
back: It fails the client focused advice criterion, because the partner is left doing the work you were asked to do. State which option you recommend and give the reasons in terms of the client's objective, not just legal merit.

front: What makes a next steps section adequate in a case and matter analysis report?
back: It must be practical, sequenced and attributable: who does what, by when, in numbered steps, including diarising any limitation date.

front: Should the report contain an ethics heading even when nothing turns on it?
back: Yes. Ethical and professional conduct issues get a separate heading, always present, even if only to record that none arises.

front: Can you depart from the default report structure?
back: Yes, and if the partner's instructions ask for a specific structure you follow the instructions. Departing from a good default is a choice; having no default at all is a handicap.

front: What earns credit under applying the law correctly?
back: Accuracy: identifying the correct legal principles and applying them accurately to the facts. Stating the wrong test, applying the right test to the wrong facts, or reaching a conclusion the law does not support loses marks here however much you have written.

front: What earns credit under applying the law comprehensively?
back: Coverage: the extent and completeness of your identification and analysis. Did you find all the issues or only the obvious one, liability as well as quantum, the limitation point, the counterclaim, the interest, the costs consequences? A report can be entirely correct on the two issues it addresses and still fail comprehensiveness because there were five.

front: What is the scheduling rule that follows from the comprehensiveness criterion?
back: Breadth before depth. List every issue you can see in the planning minutes, including the weak ones, and spread writing time across all of them. Four paragraphs of solid analysis on four issues beat sixteen paragraphs on one, and a single sentence identifying a weak point and dismissing it with a reason still shows you saw it.

front: What must you do with legal materials supplied in the bundle?
back: Use them. Where the assessment gives you standard conditions of sale, an extract from articles of association or similar materials, you are expected to apply them, and failing to apply a document that has been handed to you is a visible gap in the report.

front: In negotiation analysis, what is the difference between a position and an interest?
back: A position is what a party says they want; an interest is why they want it. A seller's position may be that they will not go below a stated price, while their interest is completing another purchase on a fixed date, which a deferred or restructured price could also satisfy. Positions collide; interests often overlap, and that overlap is where a deal lives.

front: Why assess each side's best and worst alternatives to a negotiated agreement?
back: They determine how much pressure each side is under. A client with a strong, well documented claim within limitation against a solvent defendant can negotiate firmly; a client facing expensive proceedings on contested evidence against a company with no assets cannot, and telling the partner so is client focused advice.

front: What are opening, target and reserve positions, and what else should be traded?
back: The opening is where you begin, justifiable on the facts and not so extreme it ends the conversation; the target is the realistic outcome sought; the reserve is the point below which the client should walk away and take their best alternative. Give figures and reasoning, and add non monetary terms such as timing of payment, confidentiality, continuing supply, an apology, or the treatment of costs and interest.

front: What are the ethical limits on a solicitor negotiating, and what do the NDA and SLAPP warning notices add?
back: You may press hard, decline to answer, and need not volunteer information helping the other side, but you must not mislead: no false statement of fact, no leaving a statement uncorrected once it becomes false, no permitting a misapprehension you created, and no taking unfair advantage of a third party, which is especially live where they are unrepresented. An NDA must not prevent reporting misconduct to a regulator or a crime to the police or improperly deter disclosure to a court, and aggressive correspondence designed to silence rather than resolve engages the SLAPP warning notice.

front: How long is the SQE2 legal research station, and how is it delivered?
back: Legal research lasts exactly 60 minutes and is a written station delivered on the Pearson VUE computer platform. There is no spell check, but a highlighter is available and you should use it on the source bundle. No books or notes may be brought in, because every source you need is provided.

front: In the legal research station, who is your written output addressed to, and what form does it take?
back: You write an internal note to the partner who instructed you, not a letter to the client and not an email to the other side. The note sets out your legal reasoning, identifies the key sources you relied on, and tells the partner what advice they should give the client.

front: Does the legal research station require you to record a research trail?
back: No. You are not asked to record databases searched, indexes consulted or search terms used. The assessor marks your reasoning and your advice, not your method, so minutes spent writing a trail buy nothing.

front: What is the decoy source trap that defines the legal research station?
back: You are given a bundle of primary and secondary sources, and some of the sources provided may not be relevant. Identifying which sources are relevant, and applying only those, is itself part of the assessment. Unlike every other station, you cannot assume that what you are given matters.

front: What is the commonest way candidates fail the legal research station?
back: They treat the bundle as a reading list to be summarised, working through the sources in the order given and paraphrasing each one. That gives equal weight to a binding Court of Appeal decision and to an irrelevant first instance case, and scores badly on identifying and using relevant sources and usually on applying the law correctly too.

front: In what order should you read the exercise materials in the legal research station?
back: Read the partner's question first, before you read a single source. Then read the bundle knowing what you are looking for. A source earns its place in your note only by answering the question the partner asked about the facts this client has.

front: Where does primary legislation sit in the hierarchy of authority, and what two things must you check about it?
back: An Act of Parliament comes first and binds every court, so if a statute answers the point it is your starting authority. Check commencement, because a provision enacted but not yet in force decides nothing for a client acting today. Check amendment too, because a section substituted or repealed by a later Act cannot be applied in its old form.

front: Where do statutory instruments and procedural rules sit in the hierarchy of authority?
back: Secondary legislation, meaning statutory instruments made under a power in an Act, sits below primary legislation and binds in the same way as the parent Act, within the limits of the power that made it. Procedural rules such as the Civil Procedure Rules and the Criminal Procedure Rules sit here in practical terms, supplemented by practice directions.

front: Which courts bind which in England and Wales, for the purposes of a research note?
back: The Supreme Court binds every court below it. The Court of Appeal binds the High Court, the county court and the magistrates' courts, and generally binds itself. High Court decisions bind the county court and magistrates' courts and are strongly persuasive at first instance but do not bind another High Court judge. County court and first instance tribunal decisions bind nobody.

front: Within a judgment, what part actually binds?
back: Only the ratio decidendi binds. Obiter comment persuades but does not compel, however eminent the judge, and a dissenting judgment does not bind at all. Say plainly in your note when you are relying on something that is persuasive only.

front: How should you treat a practitioner text or encyclopaedia extract included in a research bundle?
back: Secondary sources are not authority. They are a route to authority and a guide to how practitioners read it. If the bundle gives you a practitioner text alongside the statute it summarises, cite the statute and use the text only to support your reading of it.

front: What are the five checks to run on every source in a research bundle?
back: Jurisdiction, currency, commencement, level of court, and subject matter. Each check is a way a source can look authoritative while being useless to this client, and running all five is how you separate authority from decoy.

front: What is the jurisdiction check, and what is the reverse trap hidden inside it?
back: Ask whether the source is from England and Wales, because a Scottish, Northern Irish, Irish, Australian or Canadian decision is at best persuasive. The reverse trap is Wales: it is not a separate jurisdiction, but the law applying in Wales can differ from the law applying in England, so a Welsh provision may be included to see whether you noticed the client's property is in Cardiff rather than Chester.

front: What is the currency check on a source?
back: Ask whether the source has been superseded. Look for a later case in the bundle that overrules or departs from an earlier one, for a statute that has replaced the common law rule, and for a headnote recording subsequent history. Note too that a case a later court has distinguished on facts materially like your client's remains good law but no longer governs your point, so it is not the authority you want.

front: What is the commencement check, and why is an uncommenced provision such a common decoy?
back: Read commencement sections and any transitional provisions to confirm the rule is actually in force for this client. An uncommenced or transitionally limited provision reads exactly like good law, so it tempts a candidate who skipped the front and back of the extract. A rule applying only to transactions entered into after a given date does not help a client who contracted before it.

front: Why is the subject matter check the subtlest of the five decoy checks?
back: A case on the same statute but a different subsection, or the same doctrine in a different factual context, looks entirely right until you read it closely. Everything about the citation, the court and the language matches, so only reading the operative reasoning against the partner's actual question exposes it.

front: Should you tell the partner in your note that you ruled a source out, and at what length?
back: Yes, in one short line, for example that a named extract concerns a fixed term tenancy and does not assist here. That shows the assessor you read the source and exercised judgment. Do not write a paragraph rejecting each irrelevant source, and only mention a source tempting enough that the partner might otherwise raise it.

front: How should the first 20 minutes of the 60 minute research station be spent?
back: Minutes 0 to 5: read the partner's email twice, write the question in your own words as a heading, number multiple questions, and note any deadline, figure or advice the partner has already given the client. Minutes 5 to 20: read the bundle with that question in mind, highlighting as you go, and note for each source what it is and whether it is in, out or doubtful, without reading anything twice.

front: Between minutes 20 and 30 of the research station you should do the step most candidates skip. What is it?
back: Decide the answer, and write the short answer in a single sentence before you write anything else. If you cannot write that sentence, you have not finished reasoning, and more writing will not fix it. Skipping this step is why so many notes wander.

front: What should you check in the final eight minutes of the research station?
back: Check that every source cited is one you actually applied, that the advice answers the question asked, that your caveats are honest, and that any ethical issue has been resolved rather than merely mentioned. Spelling and grammar errors that do not affect legal accuracy, clarity or certainty do not cost marks, but a typo inside a citation or a figure affects all three.

front: Name the seven parts of the reusable research note structure, in order.
back: The question asked; the short answer; the relevant law with citations; application to the client's facts; the advice the partner should give the client; gaps and caveats; and ethical and professional conduct issues. The same skeleton suits any practice area and stops you drifting.

front: What belongs in the short answer section of a research note?
back: One sentence, occasionally two, giving the conclusion rather than a preview of your reasoning. A partner reading only that paragraph should be able to pick up the telephone. If the answer is conditional, say so in the same sentence, for example yes provided the notice was served before completion.

front: Which section of the research note should be the longest, and what does it have to contain?
back: Application to the client's facts is the heart of the note and should be the longest section. Name the client, use the dates, figures and documents from the file, and for each element of the test say which fact satisfies it. Where an element is not satisfied, say so and say what would change that.

front: What does client focused advice mean in a research note, given the note is written to a partner?
back: The advice section must be written so the partner can pass it straight on to the client. Say what the client should do, what the options are, what each costs or risks, and what you recommend. Client focused means answering the client's problem, not describing the law that surrounds it: a client asking whether they can withhold the last instalment wants to be told whether they can.

front: What is the difference between an honest caveat and vague hedging in a research note?
back: An honest caveat names the specific thing you do not know: a missing document, a fact to check with the client, a limitation date to confirm, an unsettled point of authority. That gains marks. Vague hedging that covers everything and commits to nothing loses them.

front: How can a conduct issue arise inside a legal research task, and what must your note do about it?
back: The partner may ask you to find support for a conclusion the sources do not support, a conflict may emerge between two clients of the firm, or material may raise confidentiality or money laundering concerns. Name the issue, identify the SRA Principle or Code duty engaged, and say what should be done. Spotting the issue and then failing to resolve it scores no better than not spotting it.

front: What should your research note say if the facts raise no ethical issue at all?
back: Do not invent one. A short line confirming that you considered professional conduct and identified no issue on these facts is enough. A manufactured conduct point wastes words and shows poor judgment.

front: Why is legal research the one SQE2 station where you can be expected to cite authority, and how should you cite?
back: Everywhere else you are not required to recall or cite authority, except where a case or provision is simply the normal name for the rule, such as Rylands v Fletcher, CPR Part 36 or a section 25 notice. Here the sources are in front of you, so citation is part of the job. Cite statutes by short title, year and provision, instruments by name and year then regulation number, rules by rule number, and cases by party names with the citation and court where the bundle gives them.

front: What are the two rules governing citation length in a research note?
back: First, cite the narrowest provision that does the work, because a reference to a whole Act tells the partner nothing. Second, do not quote at length: twenty words from the operative part of a section or from a ratio can earn their place, but three copied paragraphs demonstrate typing rather than analysis and squeeze out the application section where the marks are.

front: The research point falls outside the Functioning Legal Knowledge you revised for SQE1. What does that mean and what should you do?
back: It is deliberate, because the station exists to test whether you can handle an unfamiliar problem with the sources provided. Read the operative words slowly, identify the conditions the provision imposes, list them and check each against the facts. An unfamiliar statute answered by careful reading scores far better than a half remembered general principle, which is exactly what the decoys are designed to attract.

front: How long is the legal writing station and what do you produce?
back: Legal writing lasts exactly 30 minutes on the Pearson VUE platform, the shortest assessment in SQE2. You produce one letter or one email that could be sent as it stands, in response to an email from a partner, not an abstract piece of advice to the partner about strategy.

front: Why is the clock the first thing that makes legal writing different from the other written stations?
back: Case and matter analysis and legal research each give you 60 minutes, and legal drafting gives you 45. Legal writing gives you 30 minutes to read, plan, write and check. Candidates who approach it as a shorter case and matter analysis run out of time with the advice half delivered.

front: Who can the recipient of a legal writing letter be?
back: The recipient may be a client, a third party, the other side to litigation or to a client transaction, or a partner within your own organisation. The identity of the recipient controls almost everything about the document, and it changes from station to station.

front: What are the four skills criteria for legal writing, and what do they tell you about where the marks sit?
back: Include relevant facts; use a logical structure; advice and content is client and recipient focused; and use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient. Two of the four are about the recipient, which is more weight on audience than any other SQE2 station gives.

front: What are the three application of law criteria for legal writing?
back: Apply the law correctly to the client's situation; apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation; and identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity. Skills and application of law are weighted equally across SQE2 as a whole.

front: There is no spell check and no marking criterion for presentation. What errors still cost you marks?
back: You should not lose marks for spelling, grammar or formatting errors that do not affect legal accuracy, clarity or certainty. A typo in a party's name, a missing word not, a wrong figure or a wrong date does affect all three, so check names, numbers, dates and negatives rather than hunting stray commas.

front: How should the 30 minutes of the legal writing station be divided?
back: Roughly 6 minutes reading and planning, 20 minutes writing, and 4 minutes checking. Rehearse the division until it is automatic, because on the day you will not have spare attention to invent a plan.

front: What should you do in the first six minutes of the legal writing station?
back: Read the partner's email twice before anything else, because it gives the recipient, the purpose and the boundaries of the task, and highlight the instruction sentences. Then skim the attachments only for the facts the instruction needs. Spend the last minute or two typing a skeleton of five or six headings straight into the answer box.

front: Why should you write straight through in the 20 minute writing block rather than polishing as you go?
back: Marks for structure and completeness are much larger than marks for elegance. A letter that stops before the next steps section has thrown away a skills criterion and a large part of the application of law marks, so finishing beats refining.

front: What five checks should you run in the final four minutes of the legal writing station, in order?
back: Is every party named correctly; is every figure and date right; is every negative the right way round; have I answered every part of the partner's instruction; and have I dealt with the ethical point. Nothing else.

front: Name the seven parts of the reusable legal writing structure.
back: Salutation appropriate to the recipient; purpose; background limited to what the recipient needs; the advice or the position; options and consequences; the ask or next steps; and a sign off matching the salutation. The same structure works whoever the recipient is.

front: What does the purpose paragraph at the top of a legal writing letter do?
back: In one or two sentences it says what the letter is about and what it does, for example that you are writing to advise on the client's options following a landlord's notice of a stated date and to recommend a course of action. A reader who knows within ten seconds why the document exists reads the rest properly.

front: How much background should a legal writing letter contain?
back: Only as much as this recipient needs. A client who lived through the facts needs one line of orientation, a partner who has never seen the file needs a short factual summary, and the other side's solicitor needs only the facts you are choosing to put to them.

front: Why is listing options without evaluating them not good enough?
back: The recipient focused criteria require you to set out the realistic courses of action with the practical consequence, cost and risk of each, and to give a recommendation where the partner has asked for one. A bare list leaves the decision unmade and is not client focused.

front: What must the closing section of a legal writing letter contain?
back: A precise ask: exactly what you need from the recipient and by when, for example asking them to confirm by 4pm on a named date whether they wish you to accept. A letter that ends without an ask has not done its job, and please do not hesitate to contact me is not an ask.

front: How do the salutation and sign off pair up in a legal writing letter?
back: Yours sincerely goes with a named addressee such as Dear Mrs Achebe or Dear Ms Whitfield; Yours faithfully goes with Dear Sirs or Dear Sir or Madam. Add your name and the firm. It is a small point but the marks are free.

front: Why can two letters resting on identical legal analysis be graded completely differently?
back: Because the recipient criteria are marked separately from the application of law criteria. A letter to a distressed lay client, a letter to the other side's solicitor and an internal note to a partner are three different documents, and getting the law right does not earn the recipient marks.

front: How should you handle technical vocabulary when writing to a lay client?
back: Assume no legal knowledge and convert the terms into plain words, for example saying the seller must transfer the property free from any rights you do not know about rather than full title guarantee. Where a term genuinely is the name of the thing, such as a Part 36 offer or a section 25 notice, name it once and explain it in a clause.

front: How should a letter to a lay client handle bad news and the client's feelings?
back: Explain the outcome first and then the reason, and be honest about bad news rather than softening a weak case into a strong one, because a client misled into litigating has been badly served and the marker will see it. Where the file shows distress, acknowledge it briefly and without gushing, then give the client a decision framed so they can actually make it.

front: What register suits a letter to the other side's solicitor?
back: Formal, courteous, factual and firm. Technical terms are appropriate because you are addressing a professional, and shorthand saves words. State your client's position, the basis for it and what you require, without aggression, sarcasm or personal comment.

front: What may you never do in correspondence with the other side, however forcefully you are instructed to put your client's case?
back: You must not overstate the merits or assert something you know to be untrue, because you must not mislead another party or their representative. You must not disclose privileged material or anything the client has not authorised you to reveal.

front: When is an open letter the right vehicle in correspondence with the other side?
back: An open letter can be shown to the court, so it is right for setting out your client's case, a formal demand, a request for documents, and anything you would be happy for a judge to read. Decide whether your letter is open or without prejudice before you type the first line.

front: What is a without prejudice letter, and what does the label without prejudice save as to costs add?
back: A without prejudice letter is a genuine attempt to settle a dispute, and the protection means it generally cannot be put before the court as evidence of an admission if settlement fails. Marking it without prejudice save as to costs keeps it protected during the negotiation but allows it to be shown to the court on the question of costs after judgment.

front: Does writing without prejudice at the top of a letter create the protection?
back: No. The label does not create the protection by itself: a letter so marked that makes no settlement proposal, or that simply asserts the client's case, may not attract it, and a genuine settlement proposal may be protected even if the label was forgotten. It is the substance of a genuine attempt to settle that matters.

front: The partner asks you to make an offer to settle. Why is writing it as open correspondence a serious error?
back: An open letter can be put before the judge, so setting out a concession or explaining how weak your own client's case is hands the other side a document they can rely on. It is an error of judgment, not a formatting slip, and it will be marked as one.

front: A beneficiary of an estate writes to you asking for advice, and your firm acts for the executors. How do you reply?
back: Tell them plainly that you act for the executors, that you cannot advise them, and suggest they take their own independent advice. You must not mislead anyone into thinking you act for them, and confidentiality is owed to your client rather than to the smooth running of the correspondence, so keep to information you are authorised to give.

front: How should an internal note to a partner differ from a letter to a client?
back: It is the most technical and least explanatory of the four registers. Your reader is a solicitor, so use proper legal terminology without translation, be short, and lead with the answer: issue, short answer, analysis, risks, recommendation, next steps, and anything you need the partner to decide.

front: What can you say to a partner in an internal note that you would not put in a letter, and what limit still applies?
back: This is the recipient to whom you can say the uncomfortable things: that the client's account is inconsistent with the documents, that there is a conflict of interest, that a limitation date is close, or that the firm should consider whether it can continue to act. A note that hedges those helps nobody. It is still a document that could be disclosed in some circumstances and it is still marked for accuracy.

front: A partner's instruction, if followed exactly, would have you mislead the recipient or take unfair advantage of an unrepresented person. What is the right response in a legal writing station?
back: The right response is almost never to refuse to write anything. Write the letter properly, leave out the improper element, and tell the partner what you have done and why, either in the letter itself where the partner is the recipient or in a short covering note. Ethics are pervasive and never flagged, so no line will tell you to consider your obligations.

front: What length should a legal writing answer be, and what is the final test to apply before submitting?
back: Concise is a marked criterion, so in 20 minutes of writing aim for roughly 400 to 600 words, with short sentences, one idea per paragraph, and headings once the content has more than two strands. The final test is whether this recipient could read it once and know exactly what has happened, what it means for them, and what they now have to do.

front: How long is the legal drafting station, and what three forms can the task take?
back: Legal drafting lasts exactly 45 minutes on the Pearson VUE platform, with a highlighter and no spell check. You may be asked to draft from a precedent supplied in the materials, to amend a document already drafted, or to draft from scratch with neither a precedent nor a draft in front of you. You are asked to produce the document itself, not to advise.

front: What are the two skills criteria for legal drafting?
back: Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language, and structure the document appropriately and logically. Legal drafting is marked on five criteria in total, fewer than any other written station.

front: What are the three application of law criteria for legal drafting?
back: Draft a document which is legally correct; draft a document which is legally comprehensive; and identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.

front: Which criteria that appear in other written stations are missing from legal drafting, and why?
back: There is no client focused advice criterion and no include relevant facts criterion, because the output is a document rather than advice. Nobody reads a share purchase agreement to be advised; they read it to know what the parties agreed and what happens if it goes wrong.

front: Why should you never explain your reasoning inside a drafted document?
back: A sentence saying a clause has been included to protect the seller because the buyer raised concerns is commentary, not a clause, and it should be stripped out. If the instructions ask for a covering note or drafting note, the reasoning goes there and only there; if they do not ask for one, do not write one.

front: Why must you not soften drafted language for a lay reader, when legal writing rewards exactly that?
back: The audience for a drafted document is whoever must one day enforce it: the other side's solicitor, a judge, a Land Registry caseworker or a court office. Precision beats accessibility every time, and reasonable endeavours and best endeavours mean different things, so choosing the wrong one is a legal error rather than a stylistic one.

front: Why does an elegant but legally ineffective clause still fail the drafting station?
back: The weight sits on legally correct, meaning the clause does in law what it is meant to do, and legally comprehensive, meaning nothing the instructions require has been left out. A penalty clause a court will not enforce, a witness statement without a statement of truth, or a will clause that fails for uncertainty all fail those criteria however good the language is.

front: Negotiation is never assessed in legal drafting. What two drafting habits does that rule out?
back: Do not draft clauses hedged with the other side's likely objections, and do not offer alternative wordings in square brackets hoping the assessor will choose one. Commit to a position and draft it. Negotiation appears only in interview and attendance note, case and matter analysis, or legal writing.

front: How should the 45 minutes of the drafting station be divided?
back: Minutes 0 to 8 reading the instructions and file, minutes 8 to 14 planning the skeleton of clause headings, minutes 14 to 38 drafting, and minutes 38 to 45 checking. Most avoidable marks are lost by not having those last seven minutes.

front: What three questions should you write down in the first eight minutes of a drafting task?
back: What document am I producing, who are the parties, and what must this document achieve for my client. Read the partner's email twice first, because it tells you which document and which clauses are wanted and which are not, and skim any supplied precedent for shape rather than word by word.

front: Why is listing the clause headings before drafting anything worth four minutes?
back: The list alone secures the structure criterion and prevents the commonest structural failure, which is drafting the interesting clause first and then bolting the rest on around it.

front: You are 30 minutes in and one clause is resisting you. What should you do?
back: Leave a marker and move on to the next clause. An incomplete document with all the required clauses present in outline scores better on comprehensiveness than a perfect half, so never polish at the cost of finishing.

front: What three passes make up the checking stage of a drafting task?
back: Read the document once against the instructions, ticking off each requested item; once for internal consistency of defined terms, cross references, numbering and party names; and once for the ethics point if you have not already dealt with it.

front: How should parties be identified and labelled in a drafted document?
back: Name the document for what it is, then identify each party fully and consistently by full legal name, with a company number for a company and a registered office or address. Give each party a short label and use it without deviation: if the buyer is defined as the Buyer, never later write the purchaser.

front: What is the discipline of a definitions clause?
back: Define a term where it will be used more than once and where its meaning is not obvious, define it once in one place, and capitalise it throughout so a reader can see it is defined. Do not define a term you never use, and do not use the same word in lower case elsewhere meaning something slightly different.

front: What do recitals do, and what must never be hidden in one?
back: Recitals set out the background and the parties' purpose, and belong in agreements, deeds and transfers where context aids interpretation. They do not create obligations, so never hide an obligation in one: a recital saying the Seller will maintain the boundary fence gives nobody a right to anything. A witness statement, defence statement or board minute has no recitals.

front: What do shall or must, may, is entitled to, and will each do in a drafted clause?
back: Shall or must imposes an obligation on a named person, and you should pick one convention and hold to it. May confers a discretion or permission and never imposes a duty. Is entitled to confers a right. Will states a future fact and is a poor way to impose a duty.

front: Why is passive drafting the most common cause of an ineffective clause?
back: Every obligation needs a named actor. Notice shall be given leaves it open who must give it, so nobody is bound; the Tenant must give notice to the Landlord binds a named party and can be enforced.

front: What four things must be clear when you draft a condition precedent?
back: What the condition is, who must satisfy it, by when, and what happens if it is not satisfied by that date. A condition precedent with no consequence for failure is a trap. Typical settings are completion of a company purchase conditional on regulatory consent, or exchange conditional on a satisfactory search result.

front: What is the difference between a warranty and an indemnity, and why does it matter for the legally correct criterion?
back: A warranty is a contractual statement of fact, so if it is untrue the innocent party sues for breach and must prove and mitigate its loss. An indemnity is a promise to reimburse a defined loss pound for pound, generally outside the ordinary rules on remoteness and mitigation. They are not interchangeable, so using one where the instructions call for the other is a legal error, not a preference.

front: What are the boundary provisions of a drafted document, and why do they matter to marks?
back: They are the clauses governing the edges of the relationship: termination on stated grounds by a stated party on stated notice with stated survival, notices with addressee, address, method and deemed service, governing law and jurisdiction where there is a foreign element, and any liability caps. Candidates who run out of time drop them first, which costs comprehensiveness marks.

front: What are the execution requirements you should know for a deed, a company, an individual, and a statement of case?
back: A deed must be clear on its face that it is a deed, be validly executed, and be delivered. A company may execute by two authorised signatories or by a director in the presence of a witness. An individual's signature on a deed must be witnessed. A witness statement and a statement of case each end with a statement of truth, the latter signed by the party or its legal representative.

front: What must a compliant Part 36 offer contain, and what happens if it does not comply?
back: It must be in writing, make clear that it is made under Part 36, specify a relevant period of not less than 21 days where it is made not less than 21 days before trial, state whether it relates to the whole of the claim or to part of it or to an issue in it, and state whether it takes into account any counterclaim. If it does not comply it is just an ordinary offer and the Part 36 costs consequences fall away, which is the clearest example of a document that reads well and does nothing.

front: What are the rules for drafting a witness statement in Dispute Resolution?
back: It must be in the witness's own words and in the first person, chronological, and confined to what the witness can say of their own knowledge, identifying the source of anything said on information and belief. It ends with a statement of truth.

front: What must a defence statement contain, and what limit does the client's instruction place on you?
back: It sets out the nature of the defence including any particular defences relied on, the matters of fact on which the defendant takes issue with the prosecution and why, particulars of the matters of fact on which the defendant intends to rely for the defence, any point of law to be taken including admissibility and abuse of process, and details of any alibi witness. It must be drafted on the client's instructions, and you must not assert a positive case the client has not given you.

front: You are asked to draft a special condition in a Property Practice contract. How must it sit with the Standard Conditions of Sale?
back: The Standard Conditions will be supplied where relevant, and the special condition must be drafted to work with them, whether it varies, excludes or supplements a standard condition. Say expressly which condition you are varying rather than leaving the reader to infer it.

front: What must a legacy in a will clause contain, and what must a deed of variation satisfy?
back: A legacy must identify the beneficiary and the subject matter with certainty and should say what happens if the beneficiary predeceases the testator. A variation must be in writing, signed by the beneficiaries giving up their entitlement, made within two years of death, and not made for any consideration in money or money's worth; where the tax reading back is intended it must contain a statement that section 142 of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 applies, and a section 62(6) TCGA 1992 statement for capital gains.

front: What must a board minute and a shareholders' resolution each record?
back: A board minute needs the company, the date, those present, confirmation of quorum, any declarations of interest, the business and the resolutions passed. A shareholders' resolution must be correctly labelled ordinary or special, record the required majority, and follow the correct procedure for a meeting or a written resolution.

front: What are the three recurring failures when amending from a supplied precedent?
back: Leaving in provisions that do not fit the transaction, such as guarantor clauses where there is no guarantor, since every clause you leave in asserts the parties agreed it. Failing to change every cross reference, because deleting a clause silently breaks the numbers pointing at it. And producing a clause that is legally ineffective because the precedent reflects law or practice that does not apply, or because the amendment hollowed it out.

front: A partner asks you to draft a board minute recording a declaration of interest that was never made. What do you do, and how do you handle the ethics point generally in drafting?
back: Do not draft it, because recording something you know is untrue engages the duty not to mislead. Resolve the point in the way the instructions allow: if a covering note or email to the partner is permitted, say what the problem is, which SRA Principle or Code duty it engages and what you propose instead; if not, draft the compliant clause rather than the improper one. Silence scores nothing, and that criterion is worth as much as legal correctness.

front: In SQE2, which oral station and how many written stations does Criminal Law and Practice carry, and what is its underlying black letter law?
back: Criminal Law and Practice carries the Advocacy station on oral day 2 and two of the four written exercises on written day 1. The underlying black letter law is Criminal Liability. The practice area expressly includes advising clients at the police station.

front: What four settings does a criminal SQE2 station almost always sit in?
back: The police station, the first hearing in the magistrates' court, a bail application, or a sentencing hearing. The range of scenarios is deliberately narrow, so prepare those four thoroughly rather than reading widely.

front: Who is the custody officer and what does that officer decide when a suspect arrives?
back: The custody officer is a sergeant or above who must not be involved in the investigation. That officer decides whether there is sufficient evidence to charge and, if not, whether detention without charge is necessary to secure or preserve evidence or to obtain evidence by questioning.

front: What is the custody record and why should the solicitor read it first?
back: The custody record is opened when detention is authorised and logs every event, request and refusal during the detention. Reading it first tells you what has happened, what your client has asked for and what has been refused, which is the factual foundation for everything you then do.

front: What three continuing rights must the custody officer tell the suspect about?
back: The right to have someone informed of the arrest, the right to consult the Codes of Practice, and the right to consult a solicitor privately and free of charge at any time. They are continuing rights, so they can be exercised at any point during detention, not only at the outset.

front: Is legal advice at the police station free, and is it means tested?
