back: It is free and it is not means tested. It is also independent of the police. Say this plainly to a client who is worried about cost or who assumes the duty solicitor works with the police.

front: When does the detention clock start and what is the basic period of detention without charge?
back: The clock runs from the relevant time, which is normally arrival at the first police station. The basic period is 24 hours.

front: How can detention without charge be extended beyond 24 hours, and what is the outer limit?
back: A superintendent may extend detention to 36 hours where the offence is indictable and the conditions are met. Beyond 36 hours only a magistrates' court can authorise further detention, by warrant, to an outer limit of 96 hours.

front: Who reviews detention, and at what intervals?
back: An inspector unconnected with the investigation must review detention. The first review is within six hours of authorisation and later reviews follow at intervals of no more than nine hours.

front: Which detainees must have an appropriate adult?
back: Detainees under 18, and adults who are vulnerable because of a mental health condition or mental disorder. A vulnerable suspect must not be interviewed without an appropriate adult save in genuinely urgent situations.

front: What is the role of the appropriate adult, and is what the detainee says to them privileged?
back: The appropriate adult supports the detainee and sees that the interview is conducted properly and fairly. They give no legal advice and they are not covered by privilege, so nothing said in front of them is protected in the way advice from the solicitor is.

front: Your client at the police station cannot follow simple questions and appears unwell. Why does this earn marks?
back: Raising the appropriate adult and fitness for interview in that situation is a marked point, not a courtesy. A client who is intoxicated, very young, plainly unwell or unable to follow simple questions should not be interviewed until those issues are addressed.

front: Are the police obliged to hand over their evidence before interview?
back: There is no statutory duty to hand over their evidence at that stage. The Codes require them to give sufficient information for the suspect to understand the nature of the offence and why he is suspected of it, so you ask the investigating officer what the case is.

front: Why does thin or drip fed police disclosure support advising no comment?
back: If disclosure is thin, withheld or drip fed you cannot properly advise on what facts the client may later wish to rely on, because you do not know what the allegation is. That is a proper basis for advising no comment. State the reason on tape at the start of the interview so a court can later see that silence was the product of legal advice given for a stated reason.

front: How does full disclosure of a strong case change your advice at the police station?
back: Where disclosure is full and the case strong, an early account or an early guilty plea may serve the client best. Disclosure drives advice, so the quality of what the police have told you is the first thing you assess.

front: Set out the caution and what each of its three parts warns the suspect.
back: The caution warns the suspect that he does not have to say anything, that it may harm his defence if he does not mention when questioned something which he later relies on in court, and that anything he does say may be given in evidence. The middle limb is the source of the adverse inference from silence.

front: When may a court draw an adverse inference from a failure to mention a fact in interview?
back: Where the defendant failed to mention, when questioned under caution, a fact later relied on in his defence which he could reasonably have been expected to mention at the time. The inference bites on the mismatch between the interview and the defence run at trial.

front: What two failures to account can found an adverse inference, and what must precede them?
back: A failure to account for objects, substances or marks on the suspect or in his possession, and a failure to account for his presence at a place. Both require a special warning in ordinary language first.

front: Can an inference be drawn where the suspect was denied access to a solicitor, and can a conviction rest on an inference alone?
back: No inference may be drawn if the suspect was not allowed the opportunity to consult a solicitor before questioning. Nobody may be convicted solely on an inference.

front: Does the fact that the client was silent on legal advice defeat an adverse inference?
back: Not by itself. What may defeat it is the reason for the advice. That is why the reason must be sound and must be recorded at the start of the interview.

front: A further adverse inference provision applies at trial. What is it?
back: An inference may be drawn from a failure to give evidence at trial. It sits alongside the interview based inferences, and the same rule applies that nobody may be convicted solely on an inference.

front: What are the three realistic options for a suspect facing interview?
back: Answering questions, handing in a prepared statement and then answering no further questions, or making no comment. Each is chosen for a reason you can articulate, and the reason is what a marker is looking for.

front: When does answering questions in interview suit the client?
back: Where the client has a clear, truthful, exculpatory account which he can give under pressure, where disclosure is sufficient to know what that account must meet, and where there is a realistic chance of no charge.

front: What is a prepared statement and what does it achieve?
back: You draft it, the client adopts it, it is handed in, usually at the start of interview, and he answers no further questions. It puts the facts relied on on the record, protecting against an adverse inference, while sparing him cross examination in an interview room.

front: What is the cost of using a prepared statement?
back: Commitment. The account is fixed early, before real disclosure, and any later departure from it is material for cross examination. Advise the client of that before he adopts it.

front: When does no comment suit the client, and why is it not a default?
back: It suits inadequate disclosure, an unfit or vulnerable client, a client who cannot yet give a coherent account, or police who plainly have insufficient evidence and are fishing. It is not a default because you must be able to articulate the reason, and you must tell the client honestly that a court may later be invited to hold the silence against him.

front: What is the starting presumption on bail?
back: A defendant is entitled to bail unless an exception applies. Structure every bail argument from that presumption, so the burden is on the prosecution to bring the case within an exception.

front: What are the main bail exceptions for an imprisonable either way or indictable offence?
back: Substantial grounds for believing that if released the defendant would fail to surrender, would commit further offences on bail, or would interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct the course of justice. Others include detention for his own protection and the court having insufficient information.

front: What extra protection exists for an adult with no previous convictions?
back:
FRONT: What extra protection exists for an adult who has not been convicted in the present proceedings?
BACK: Where an adult has not been convicted of an offence in those proceedings and there is no real prospect that he will receive a custodial sentence in them, there are additional restrictions on refusing him bail. Note that previous convictions from earlier, unrelated matters do not take the point away, so take it expressly wherever custody is not a realistic outcome, because it narrows what the prosecution can rely on.

front: What statutory factors are used to establish a bail ground, and what is the trap?
back: The nature and seriousness of the offence and likely disposal, the defendant's character, antecedents, associations and community ties, his record of compliance with bail, and the strength of the evidence. The trap is treating a factor as a ground. Factors feed a ground; they are not grounds themselves.

front: List the bail conditions available and the test each must satisfy.
back: Residence, a curfew with or without electronic monitoring, reporting to a police station, no direct or indirect contact with named witnesses, exclusion from an area, surrender of a passport, a security or a surety. Every condition must be necessary for a statutory purpose, and the persuasive advocate offers a package answering each objection raised.

front: How do you structure a bail application in the Advocacy station?
back: Introduce yourself, your client and the application. State the charge and the stage shortly. Take the objections in the order raised and answer each, deploying the statutory factors and then the condition that neutralises the risk. Close by inviting the court to grant bail on the conditions offered, and be ready for questions from the bench, because engaging with the judge is itself an assessed skill.

front: What can be done after the magistrates refuse bail?
back: Two full applications are normally available, and any further application requires a change of circumstances. A magistrates' refusal can be appealed to the Crown Court.

front: Where are summary only and indictable only offences tried, and which offences need allocation?
back: Summary only offences are tried in the magistrates' court. Indictable only offences are sent to the Crown Court at the first hearing with no consideration of venue. Only either way offences require allocation.

front: What happens at plea before venue?
back: The charge is put and the defendant indicates a plea. On a guilty indication the magistrates sentence, or commit to the Crown Court for sentence if their powers are insufficient. On a not guilty indication, or none, the court moves to allocation.

front: What does the court do at the allocation stage of an either way offence?
back: It hears the prosecution, which informs the court of previous convictions, and the defence, applies the Allocation Guideline, and decides whether its sentencing powers are adequate. If it declines jurisdiction the case is sent up; if it accepts jurisdiction the defendant is told he may consent to summary trial or elect trial by jury.

front: Advise on electing Crown Court trial: what points go each way, and who decides?
back: For the Crown Court: trial by jury, higher acquittal rates on some offence types, a judge ruling on admissibility separately from the tribunal of fact, and fuller disclosure. Against: delay, cost, stress, and materially greater sentencing power. Give the advice, then let the client decide, because election is his choice, not yours.

front: What is the magistrates' maximum sentence for a single either way offence?
back: Do not memorise a figure. That limit has been altered more than once in recent years, so check the limit current at your sitting. The principle to carry into the exam is that the magistrates' powers are capped and that a defendant tried summarily may still be committed to the Crown Court for sentence.

front: What happens at the magistrates' first hearing on a not guilty plea, and what is the overriding objective?
back: The prosecution provides initial details of its case, the defendant enters his plea, and the court completes a case management form identifying the real issues, the witnesses genuinely required, and the directions and time limits. The overriding objective is that criminal cases be dealt with justly, and the parties must actively assist the court in managing the case.

front: What is the plea and trial preparation hearing?
back: The first Crown Court hearing before a judge, ordinarily within a few weeks of sending. The defendant is arraigned, directions are given and a trial date is fixed.

front: State the prosecutor's statutory disclosure duty.
back: The prosecutor must disclose material which might reasonably be capable of undermining the prosecution case or assisting the defence. The duty is continuing, so it does not end when initial disclosure is served.

front: What is a defence statement, where is it compulsory, and what does it trigger?
back: It sets out the nature of the defence, the matters of fact in issue and the reasons for them. It is compulsory in the Crown Court and voluntary in the magistrates' court. It triggers the prosecutor's review of unused material and any application for specific disclosure.

front: State the elements of theft, and explain how a defendant can steal his own goods.
back: Theft is the dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with the intention permanently to deprive. Appropriation is the assumption of any of the rights of an owner and can occur even with the owner's consent. Property belonging to another covers property in which another has any proprietary right or interest, which is how a defendant can steal goods he owns.

front: How is dishonesty established in theft?
back: A defendant is not dishonest if he believes he has a legal right to the property, that the owner would have consented had he known, or that the owner cannot be discovered by taking reasonable steps. Beyond those, first find his actual knowledge or belief as to the facts, then ask whether his conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people. There is no longer any requirement that he realised he was dishonest by those standards.

front: State the elements of robbery, and what happens if the theft fails.
back: Robbery is theft plus force. The prosecution must prove a complete theft, and that immediately before or at the time of it, and in order to steal, the defendant used force on a person or put or sought to put a person in fear of being then and there subjected to force. If the theft fails, the offence is not robbery.

front: What are the two forms of burglary?
back: First, entering a building or part of a building as a trespasser with intent to steal, inflict grievous bodily harm or cause criminal damage, the intent existing at entry. Second, having entered as a trespasser, stealing or attempting to steal, or inflicting or attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm.

front: State the elements of fraud by false representation and when the offence is complete.
back: Dishonestly making a false representation, knowing it is or might be untrue or misleading, with intent to make a gain or cause a loss or expose another to a risk of loss. It is complete when the representation is made: nobody need be deceived and no gain need result. A representation may be express or implied, and may be made to a machine.

front: What must be proved for assault occasioning actual bodily harm?
back: An assault or battery causing harm that is more than trifling. The mental element is only that of the assault or battery itself, so no intention or foresight of the harm is needed.

front: Distinguish the two grievous bodily harm offences, and define a wound.
back: Unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting grievous bodily harm requires intention or recklessness as to some harm, not serious harm. The more serious offence is wounding or causing grievous bodily harm with intent to do grievous bodily harm or to resist or prevent lawful arrest, where nothing short of that intent will do. A wound is a break in both layers of the skin.

front: State the elements of criminal damage and its two statutory lawful excuses.
back: Destroying or damaging property belonging to another, intending to do so or being reckless as to whether it is done, without lawful excuse. The statutory lawful excuses cover a belief that the owner would have consented, and acting to protect other property, both judged on the facts as the defendant honestly believed them to be.

front: What is aggravated criminal damage, and where must the danger come from?
back: Damaging property intending or being reckless as to whether life is thereby endangered. It is far more serious than simple criminal damage, and the danger must arise from the damage itself.

front: State the test for self defence.
back: A defendant may use force that is reasonable in the circumstances as he honestly believed them to be, to defend himself or another, to protect property or to prevent crime. The honesty of the belief is subjective; the reasonableness of the response is objective on those believed facts, allowing for the fact that a person acting in the heat of the moment cannot weigh matters to a nicety.

front: What must be shown for duress by threats, and how is the defence lost?
back: Threats of death or serious injury, a reasonable belief in them, and a response the sober person of reasonable firmness sharing the defendant's characteristics would have made. It is lost by voluntary association with those known to be capable of coercion, and it is no defence to murder.

front: What is the effect of voluntary intoxication, and when is consent a defence?
back: Voluntary intoxication may negate the intent required for a specific intent offence but not the recklessness sufficient for a basic intent offence. Consent is a defence to assault and battery but not ordinarily to the deliberate infliction of actual bodily harm or worse, subject to recognised exceptions such as properly conducted sport, surgery and tattooing.

front: What steps does a Sentencing Council guideline take the court through, and how binding is it?
back: Assess culpability and harm to reach a category, take the category starting point and range, adjust for aggravating and mitigating factors, apply the reduction for a guilty plea, then consider totality, ancillary orders such as compensation, and credit for time on remand. The court must follow the relevant guideline unless satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.

front: Give the common aggravating and mitigating factors at sentence.
back: Aggravating: previous convictions, especially recent and similar, offending on bail, hostility based on a protected characteristic, offending in a group, the vulnerability of the victim, and being under the influence. Mitigating: good character, genuine remorse, a subordinate role, mental disorder or learning disability, sole or primary caring responsibilities, and steps taken to address offending.

front: How does credit for a guilty plea work, and how does it differ from remorse?
back: Credit is separate from remorse. The maximum reduction is available for an indication at the first stage and slides downwards thereafter. Remorse is a mitigating factor applied when the court adjusts within the category range; plea credit is a discount applied afterwards.

front: State the custody threshold and what the court must then consider.
back: A custodial sentence may be passed only where the offence is so serious that neither a fine nor a community sentence can be justified. Even then the court must consider whether the sentence can be suspended.

front: What are the three parts of a plea in mitigation?
back: First the offence: accept what must be accepted and place the offending at the lowest defensible point in the guideline, using the role, the absence of planning, the limited harm and the absence of weapons. Second the offender: humanise the client with the facts a sentencer acts on, such as work, dependants, health and steps taken since the offence. Third the sentence: say what you want and how the court can properly get there. Never sit down without naming the outcome you seek.

front: Your client admits guilt but insists on pleading not guilty. What may you do and what may you not do?
back: You may continue to act, put the prosecution to proof, test its witnesses and submit that the evidence does not reach the criminal standard. You may not advance a positive case inconsistent with the admission, so you cannot suggest he was elsewhere, call him to deny it, or suggest someone else did it. Explain that limit, and if he insists on an approach you cannot properly take, cease to act.

front: Your client proposes to give false evidence, or to call a witness he tells you will lie. What must you do?
back: He cannot be assisted. You must not mislead the court or allow it to be misled, so if he will not be dissuaded you must withdraw. Withdraw without revealing the reason, because confidentiality survives the end of the retainer.

front: When do co-defendants create a conflict, and how does confidentiality sit against the duty to the court?
back: You cannot act for two clients where there is a conflict of interest or a significant risk of one, and the risk crystallises the moment one client's account shifts blame onto the other or one is minded to give evidence against him; if you hold confidential information from both you will normally have to stop acting for both. Where confidentiality to one client conflicts with the duty to make another aware of material information, confidentiality prevails. Above both sits the duty to the court: do not mislead it, do not knowingly put forward false information, and correct any misleading impression you have created.

front: What is distinctive about Dispute Resolution's place in the SQE2 assessment pattern?
back: It is one of only two practice areas carrying an advocacy station, the other being Criminal Litigation, and it carries two written stations as well. The advocacy station is 45 minutes of preparation and 15 minutes before a solicitor playing a judge, almost always on an interim application. The underlying law is contract and tort.

front: What five questions must be answered before anything is drafted on a new claim?
back: The cause of action, limitation, the parties, the remedy, and the merits. Working through all five in order is what turns a set of facts into advice a client can act on.

front: Why must the cause of action be named precisely?
back: Breach of an express term differs from breach of a term implied by the Sale of Goods Act 1979 or the Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982, and negligence is different again. Where the client has both a contractual and a tortious route, say which is better, because the damages measure and the limitation period may differ.

front: What is the ordinary limitation period for contract and tort claims, and when does time start in each?
back: Ordinarily six years from accrual under the Limitation Act 1980. In contract time runs from the breach, not from discovery of the loss. In tort it runs from the damage, which is why the date can be later.

front: What is the limitation period for personal injury?
back: Three years from the injury or from the date of knowledge, whichever is later, with a judicial discretion to extend. Identify which trigger applies on your facts before advising that a claim is time barred.

front: How do you correctly identify a defendant as a legal person?
back: A sole trader is sued in their own name, a partnership in the firm name, and a company by its registered name and number. Getting this wrong at issue is a problem that limitation may make impossible to cure.

front: What remedies should be considered beyond damages?
back: Damages are the default, but consider specific performance, an injunction, a declaration, rescission and recovery of a debt. Choosing the remedy shapes the claim form and the particulars.

front: What does a candid view on the merits have to cover?
back: The evidential gaps, the defendant's likely answer, the litigation risk, and how that compares with the likely recovery and the irrecoverable costs. The client wants to know whether to fight, so give a view rather than a list of possibilities.

front: What governs pre action conduct, and what must a letter of claim contain?
back: Every claim is governed either by an approved pre action protocol or by the Practice Direction on Pre Action Conduct and Protocols. The letter of claim sets out the facts, the basis of the claim, what is claimed and how any sum is calculated, with the key documents.

front: What must a defendant's pre action response do?
back: Respond within the protocol period, admitting or denying each allegation with reasons, and disclosing the documents it relies on. The parties then consider settling and narrowing the issues.

front: What are the consequences of failing to comply with pre action conduct requirements?
back: Non compliance rarely bars issuing, but the court takes it into account on costs. A claimant who issues without a proper letter of claim may be deprived of costs or interest, or ordered to pay costs; a defendant who ignores one risks indemnity costs and enhanced interest.

front: Can the court order parties into a non court dispute resolution process?
back: Yes. Following the Court of Appeal's decision in Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council and the Civil Procedure Rules amendments made in October 2024, the court can order parties to engage in a non court dispute resolution process, provided the order does not impair the essence of the right to a fair trial and is proportionate.

front: What are the features of mediation, and what are the alternatives to it?
back: Mediation is voluntary in outcome, confidential and conducted without prejudice, and the mediator has no power to impose a result. The alternatives are early neutral evaluation, expert determination, arbitration, adjudication and ombudsman schemes.

front: What factors decide whether a refusal to engage in ADR was unreasonable?
back: The nature of the dispute, the merits, whether other settlement methods were tried, whether ADR costs would have been disproportionate, whether delay would have prejudiced the trial, and whether the process had a reasonable prospect of success. A winning party can be deprived of some or all of its costs if it unreasonably refused to engage.

front: Your client wants to ignore the other side's mediation invitation. What do you advise?
back: Silence in the face of an invitation is generally unreasonable in itself, and would put the client's costs at risk even if it wins. Answer every ADR invitation in writing with reasons, and keep that correspondence open so it can be shown to the judge on costs.

front: When do proceedings start, and what decides whether to issue in the County Court or the High Court?
back: Proceedings start when the court issues a claim form. Jurisdiction turns on value and complexity: money claims must generally start in the County Court unless the claimant expects to recover more than the relevant threshold, and a claim should only start in the High Court if value, complexity, importance or public interest justifies it.

front: What is the money threshold above which a claim may be started in the High Court?
back: Do not state a figure from memory. The chapter deliberately withholds it, and the threshold is a lower figure for personal injury than for other money claims. Check the current thresholds at your sitting; the examinable principle is that value plus complexity, importance or public interest is what justifies the High Court.

front: How is the High Court divided?
back: Into three divisions: the King's Bench Division, the Chancery Division and the Family Division. The specialist business and property lists across the King's Bench and Chancery Divisions are grouped as the Business and Property Courts, which is not itself a division. Identify the right division and list before advising a client that a claim will be issued in the High Court.

front: What are the time limits for serving a claim form and particulars of claim?
back: A claim form must be served within four months of issue, or six months out of the jurisdiction. Particulars of claim are served with the claim form or within fourteen days after it, and in any event within the period for serving the claim form.

front: What are the permitted methods of service, and what is the trap on timing?
back: Personal service, first class post or document exchange to the last known residence or a company's registered office, and electronic service where the recipient has confirmed in writing that it will accept it. The trap is deemed service: the deemed date follows from the method, so calculate it rather than assuming actual receipt.

front: How long does a defendant have to respond, and how is that period extended?
back: Fourteen days from service of the particulars of claim to file a defence or an acknowledgment of service. Filing an acknowledgment extends the defence deadline to twenty eight days from service of the particulars.

front: How is jurisdiction disputed?
back: By filing an acknowledgment of service and then applying within fourteen days of filing it. Filing a defence instead of taking that route risks submitting to the jurisdiction.

front: What four responses are open to a defendant, and what is special about a counterclaim?
back: Admit the whole claim, admit part, defend, or defend and counterclaim. A counterclaim is a claim in its own right, so it needs its own statement of truth and its own fee.

front: When is default judgment available and how is it entered?
back: Where the defendant files nothing in time. It is entered administratively for a specified sum, and after a damages hearing for an unspecified sum.

front: On what grounds can default judgment be set aside?
back: It must be set aside if it was wrongly entered. It may be set aside where the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending the claim or there is some other good reason, with promptness weighing heavily in the court's decision.

front: What documents are statements of case, and what is their function?
back: The claim form, particulars of claim, defence, any reply, any counterclaim and defence to it, and further information about them. Their function is to define the issues, so each party knows the case it must meet and the court knows what it must decide. They contain a concise statement of the facts relied on, not evidence and not argument.

front: What must a defence do with each allegation, and what happens if an allegation is ignored?
back: It must state which allegations are admitted, which are denied with reasons and the defendant's own version, and which are not admitted for want of knowledge. An allegation not dealt with may be taken as admitted.

front: What is a statement of truth and what is the risk in signing one?
back: Every statement of case needs a statement of truth verifying that the facts stated are believed to be true. Signing one without an honest belief in its truth exposes the signatory to contempt proceedings.

front: What happens after defences are filed, and how many allocation tracks are there?
back: The court provisionally allocates the claim and sends out directions questionnaires. There are four tracks: the small claims track, the fast track, the intermediate track and the multi track.

front: What are the features of the small claims track?
back: It takes claims of modest value, with a lower ceiling for the damages element of personal injury claims. Procedure is simplified and standard directions are given. Costs recovery is very restricted, broadly to court fees, fixed commencement costs and limited witness expenses.

front: What are the features of the fast track?
back: It takes claims above the small claims limit up to the fast track ceiling, where trial will last no more than one day and expert evidence is limited to one expert per party in no more than two fields. Fixed recoverable costs apply, set by the complexity band assigned to the claim and by the stage reached.

front: What are the monetary thresholds separating the four allocation tracks?
back: Do not state figures from memory. The chapter deliberately declines to give them because they move, so check the thresholds current at your sitting. What is examinable is the shape: value, trial length, number of parties and permitted expert evidence together decide the track, and each track carries its own costs regime.

front: What are the features of the intermediate track?
back: Introduced in October 2023, it sits between the fast track and the multi track. It takes claims above the fast track ceiling up to the intermediate ceiling where trial will last no more than three days, there are no more than three parties and oral expert evidence is limited to two experts per party. It runs on fixed recoverable costs by complexity band.

front: What are the features of the multi track?
back: It takes everything not falling into the other three tracks. Directions are tailored, often at a case management conference. Costs are assessed rather than fixed, and costs budgeting normally applies.

front: State the test for summary judgment.
back: It is available to either party where the respondent has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim, defence or issue, and there is no other compelling reason for a trial. Real means more than fanciful.

front: When will the court refuse summary judgment, and how should the application be argued?
back: The court holds no mini trial and will refuse where the case turns on disputed oral evidence or where documents are reasonably expected to become available. Argue it by isolating the issue that decides the case and showing the respondent's answer to it is not credible on the material before the court.

front: On what grounds may a statement of case be struck out?
back: Where it discloses no reasonable grounds for bringing or defending the claim, where it is an abuse of process or likely to obstruct the just disposal of proceedings, or where a rule, practice direction or order has not been complied with.

front: How do you keep strike out and summary judgment apart?
back: Strike out looks at the pleading as it stands. Summary judgment looks at the evidence. If the pleading would fail even if every fact in it were true, strike out is the application; if the pleading is adequate but the evidence cannot support it, summary judgment is.

front: When may the court order an interim payment, and how much may it order?
back: The court must be satisfied that the defendant has admitted liability, or that judgment has been obtained with damages to be assessed, or that the claimant would obtain judgment for a substantial sum. Any order must be for a reasonable proportion of the likely final judgment.

front: Set out the American Cyanamid approach to an interim injunction.
back: Is there a serious issue to be tried? Would damages adequately compensate the applicant if the injunction is refused and it later succeeds? Would the cross undertaking in damages adequately protect the respondent if it is granted and the applicant later fails? If those do not decide it, where does the balance of convenience lie, and if that is even, preserve the status quo.

front: What two duties attach to an applicant for an interim injunction, and when does the second apply?
back: A cross undertaking in damages is required as the ordinary price of the injunction, though the court retains a discretion to dispense with it, most commonly where a public body seeks the order to enforce the law. On a without notice application the applicant also owes a duty of full and frank disclosure, including of the points against it.

front: When does relief from sanctions arise, and what are the three Denton stages?
back: It arises where a party has failed to comply with a rule, practice direction or order carrying a sanction. Assess the seriousness and significance of the breach; consider why the default occurred; then evaluate all the circumstances so as to deal justly with the application, giving particular weight to the need for litigation to be conducted efficiently and at proportionate cost and to enforce compliance. Apply promptly, be candid about the cause, and show what has already been done to put it right.

front: What is the running order for any interim application before the judge?
back: Tell the judge what order you seek, then the rule, then the test, then the facts against each limb of the test, then costs. Deal with the point against you before the judge finds it.

front: What is disclosure, and what does standard disclosure require?
back: Disclosure is the statement that a document exists or has existed. Standard disclosure requires a party to disclose the documents it relies on, documents adversely affecting its own or another party's case or supporting another party's case, and documents required by a practice direction, after a reasonable and proportionate search.

front: Distinguish legal advice privilege from litigation privilege, and say who can waive privilege.
back: Legal advice privilege covers confidential communications between lawyer and client for the purpose of legal advice. Litigation privilege covers communications with third parties where litigation was in reasonable contemplation and the dominant purpose was that litigation. Privilege belongs to the client, and only the client can waive it.

front: How should without prejudice correspondence be marked, and what must you never do with it?
back: Without prejudice correspondence is privileged and cannot be put before the court on the substantive issues. Mark it "without prejudice save as to costs" where you want to rely on it on costs, which is the basis on which Part 36 operates. Never dress an open threat as a without prejudice offer.

front: What are the requirements for a witness statement, and what happens if one is served late?
back: Statements stand as evidence in chief. They must be in the witness's own words, confined to facts within the witness's own knowledge, and must identify anything said from information or belief together with its source. Exchange is usually simultaneous, and a statement served late cannot be relied on without relief from sanctions.

front: What controls expert evidence, and to whom does the expert owe a duty?
back: Expert evidence is restricted to what is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings and needs the court's permission. The expert's duty to the court overrides any duty to the instructing party. Reports must state the substance of instructions, the range of opinion, and carry a statement of truth.

front: What must a Part 36 offer contain to be a valid Part 36 offer?
back: It must state that it is made under Part 36, specify a relevant period of not less than 21 days, and say whether it relates to the whole claim or part and whether any counterclaim is taken into account. Miss any of those and the offer will not attract the Part 36 costs consequences.

front: On what basis is a Part 36 offer made, and when does the trial judge see it?
back: It is made without prejudice except as to costs. It is not put before the trial judge until everything except costs has been decided.

front: What are the costs consequences for a claimant who accepts a defendant's Part 36 offer, in time and late?
back: A claimant accepting within the relevant period recovers its costs to the date of acceptance. A claimant accepting late normally pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period to the date of acceptance; a claimant who goes to trial and fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than the offer normally pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, with interest on those costs.

front: What happens where a defendant fails to beat a claimant's own Part 36 offer?
back: The court will normally order interest on the sum awarded at a rate not exceeding ten per cent above base rate, indemnity costs from the end of the relevant period, interest on those costs at the same enhanced rate, and an additional amount calculated as a percentage of the sum awarded, subject to a cap. Those orders follow unless the court considers it unjust to make them.

front: How do you advise a client on the level at which to pitch a Part 36 offer?
back: A well pitched claimant's offer transfers risk to the defendant. Advise on the cost of continuing, the range of likely outcomes, and the offer that maximises pressure while remaining one the client would genuinely accept, because an offer the client would refuse is no protection at all.

front: What is the general rule on costs, and what tempers it?
back: Costs follow the event, so the unsuccessful party pays the successful party's costs. The court retains a discretion and will weigh conduct, exaggeration, partial success and Part 36.

front: Distinguish the standard basis from the indemnity basis of costs assessment.
back: Standard basis assessment allows only costs that are proportionate and reasonably incurred, and doubt is resolved in favour of the paying party. Indemnity basis assessment drops the proportionality test and resolves doubt in favour of the receiving party, so it is materially more generous.

front: How do costs budgets work in the multi track?
back: In most multi track cases the parties file and exchange costs budgets. The budget as agreed or approved sets the figure the court will normally allow on assessment, so an unapproved overspend is usually irrecoverable. Fast track and intermediate track claims are instead governed by fixed recoverable costs.

front: What are the routes to enforcing a money judgment?
back: Taking control of goods by a County Court warrant or a High Court writ, a third party debt order attaching a bank account or a debt owed to the debtor, a charging order over land or securities followed by an order for sale, an attachment of earnings order, and winding up a company on an undisputed debt. Enforcement is a separate exercise from obtaining judgment.

front: What is needed to form a contract, and how may terms get into it?
back: Offer, acceptance, consideration, certainty and an intention to create legal relations. Terms may be express, incorporated by signature, notice or course of dealing, or implied by fact, custom or statute.

front: Why does classifying a broken term matter, and what is the test for an innominate term?
back: Classification as a condition, a warranty or an innominate term decides whether the innocent party may terminate as well as claim damages. For an innominate term the test is whether the breach deprives that party of substantially the whole benefit of the contract.

front: How are contract damages measured, and when are they too remote?
back: Damages put the claimant in the position it would have occupied had the contract been performed, measured by expectation loss or, where that is too speculative, reliance loss. Losses are too remote unless they arise naturally from the breach or were within the parties' reasonable contemplation when they contracted.

front: State the elements of negligence and how breach, causation and remoteness are tested.
back: A duty of care, breach, causation and loss that is not too remote. Breach is measured against the reasonable person doing that activity, with a professional judged by the standard of a reasonably competent member of that profession. Causation in fact is the but for test, causation in law asks whether an intervening act broke the chain, and remoteness turns on reasonable foreseeability of the kind of damage.

front: How do contributory negligence and mitigation limit what a claimant recovers?
back: Contributory negligence reduces damages by a just and equitable proportion where the claimant's own fault contributed to the harm. Mitigation applies in both contract and tort: the claimant cannot recover loss it could reasonably have avoided, though the burden of proving a failure to mitigate falls on the defendant.

front: What is a SLAPP, what are its warning signs, and what do you do if a client asks for one?
back: A SLAPP is the use or threat of litigation to silence, intimidate or exhaust a defendant publishing on a matter of public interest, rather than to vindicate a genuine legal right. The warning signs are a weak claim pursued against an individual or small publisher, aggressive and disproportionate correspondence, labelling ordinary letters confidential or without prejudice to deter publication, and running up costs to exhaust the other side. Do not send such letters and do not pursue such a claim; advise the client that you cannot act in that way, record the advice, and decline the instruction.

front: List the stages of a freehold residential transaction in order.
back: Take instructions and verify identity, then the seller's solicitor issues the pre contract package. The buyer investigates title, raises enquiries, commissions searches and arranges finance. Contracts are then exchanged and a completion date fixed, pre completion searches are made and the certificate of title submitted, completion follows, and finally the tax is dealt with and the transfer and any charge are registered.

front: What does the seller's solicitor include in the pre contract package?
back: Official copies of the register and title plan, the draft contract, and the protocol forms. Those are typically the property information form and the fittings and contents form, plus the leasehold information form on a leasehold sale.

front: What funding questions should you ask a buyer client at the interview?
back: Ask how the purchase is financed and where every part of the money comes from, whether anyone else is contributing, and whether anyone else will live at the property. Also ask about a related sale, any chain, and what the deadline is and why. The answers drive the money laundering, occupier and co ownership advice.

front: A client asks at interview how much tax they will pay on the purchase. How do you answer?
back: Never quote a figure from memory. Explain that the amount depends on the price and on whether any relief applies, that you will calculate it using the applicable rates, and that you will confirm the figure in writing. Client care and costs information should also cover the disbursements, how the firm charges and the complaints route.

front: What is the compulsory identity requirement when taking instructions?
back: Identify the client and verify that identity from a reliable, independent source before establishing the business relationship. Naming this step expressly earns marks in an attendance note.

front: What are the three parts of a register of title and what does each contain?
back: The property register describes the land, states whether the estate is freehold or leasehold, refers to the title plan, and records rights benefiting the land such as a right of way. The proprietorship register gives the class of title, names the registered proprietor and records restrictions. The charges register records burdens such as legal charges, restrictive covenants, easements burdening the land, notices and leases.

front: Name the four classes of registered title, and say which a buyer and lender expect.
back: Absolute, good leasehold, qualified and possessory. Absolute is what a buyer and a lender expect. Anything less may require indemnity insurance or the lender's consent.

front: What does the title plan show, and what does it not show?
back: It shows the extent of the land, normally edged red. It shows general boundaries only and does not fix the precise boundary line.

front: Distinguish a notice from a restriction on the register.
back: A notice protects the priority of a third party interest, such as an option or an equitable easement. A restriction in the proprietorship register controls whether a disposition can be registered at all. Where a restriction requires a third party's consent or certificate, obtain it before completion or the application will be rejected.

front: What does a form A restriction signal, and what must the buyer's solicitor do about it?
back: It signals a tenancy in common in equity, so a sole surviving registered proprietor cannot give a good receipt for capital money. A second trustee must be appointed so that the equitable interests are overreached.

front: Which overriding interest matters most in practice, and how do you deal with it?
back: The interest of a person in actual occupation, because it binds a buyer without appearing on the register. Ask at interview and again in enquiries who occupies and who contributed to the price. Where an adult occupier is not a seller, take a signed release or have them join in the transfer.

front: What does the local search reveal?
back: Matters recorded by the local authority: planning permissions and refusals, building regulation approvals, enforcement notices, tree preservation orders, conservation area status, and whether the road is adopted.

front: What do the drainage and water enquiries and the environmental search answer, and who is responsible for a survey?
back: Drainage and water enquiries confirm connection to mains water and a public sewer, and whether a sewer runs within the boundary. An environmental search assesses contaminated land and flood risk. A survey is the buyer's own responsibility, and the lender's valuation is not a survey.

front: Why does caveat emptor make pre contract enquiries essential?
back: The buyer investigates and the buyer asks. Enquiries of the seller cover occupiers, neighbour disputes, guarantees, alterations and the consents obtained for them, services and rights of way. A seller who answers dishonestly may be liable in misrepresentation, but a buyer who never asked has no remedy.

front: What must a contract for the sale of land contain to be valid, and what does it typically set out?
back: It must be in writing, incorporate all agreed terms and be signed by or for each party. It identifies the parties, the property, the estate sold, the price, the deposit, the completion date, the title guarantee and what is included in the sale.

front: How do the standard conditions and the special conditions fit together, and which set applies where?
back: The contract incorporates standard conditions as amended by special conditions. The Standard Conditions of Sale are used residentially and the Standard Commercial Property Conditions commercially. Both will be given to you in the assessment materials, so apply the extract in front of you rather than reciting condition numbers from memory.

front: When does a seller sell with limited rather than full title guarantee?
back: Where the seller has limited knowledge of the property, for example a personal representative selling from an estate. Full title guarantee is the norm for a seller who has owned and occupied the property.

front: What must be in place before you authorise exchange of contracts?
back: The client's express authority, satisfactory title, satisfactory searches and enquiries, a mortgage offer in place, cleared deposit funds, and in a chain a synchronised completion date. Exchanging without any of these exposes both the client and the firm.

front: How does telephone exchange under a Law Society formula work?
back: Each solicitor undertakes to hold their client's signed part of the contract to the other's order and to post it the same day. The undertaking is personally binding on the solicitor who gives it.

front: In what capacity is the deposit held under the standard conditions, and why does it matter?
back: The deposit is customarily 10 per cent of the price and is held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder. A stakeholder cannot release the money before completion. It can be released early only if the contract makes the seller's solicitor agent for the seller.

front: Under each set of standard conditions, who bears the risk between exchange and completion?
back: They differ, and this is a favourite examination point. Under the Standard Conditions of Sale the seller retains the risk until completion and must transfer the property in the same physical state as at exchange, fair wear and tear excepted, and the buyer may rescind if the property becomes unusable for its purpose. Under the Standard Commercial Property Conditions risk passes to the buyer on exchange, so insurance must be in place from exchange. The old common law rule matched the commercial position, which is why the residential rule catches people out.

front: A party fails to complete on the contractual completion date. What is the first step and what does it achieve?
back: Time is not initially of the essence, so the innocent party serves a notice to complete. Under the standard conditions that makes time of the essence and gives a fixed further period, commonly ten working days, with compensation payable at the contract rate.

front: What remedies follow when a notice to complete expires unsatisfied?
back: A seller may rescind, forfeit the deposit, resell the property and claim damages for any further loss. A buyer may rescind, recover the deposit with interest and claim damages, or instead seek specific performance to compel the seller to complete.

front: Which searches are made immediately before completion, and why?
back: An official search of the whole title with priority, which confirms no new entries and confers a priority period within which to register. A bankruptcy search is made against the buyer for the lender.

front: Which transfer form is used, and what makes a document a valid deed?
back: A Land Registry form TR1 transfers the whole of a registered title and a TP1 transfers part. A deed must be clear on its face that it is a deed, be signed before a witness who attests the signature, and be delivered.

front: State the registration deadlines a buyer's solicitor must diarise, and the consequence of missing the first registration deadline.
back: An application to register a dealing with a registered title must be made within the priority period conferred by the official search, or priority is lost. A charge created by a company must also be registered at Companies House within 21 days of creation. Where the transaction triggers first registration, the application must be made within two months of completion, failing which the transfer becomes void as regards the legal estate, which reverts to the seller to hold on a bare trust for the buyer.

front: Which land transaction tax applies in England and which in Wales, and who administers each?
back: A land transaction in England attracts stamp duty land tax, administered by HM Revenue and Customs. A land transaction in Wales attracts land transaction tax, administered by the Welsh Revenue Authority. They are genuinely different taxes with different legislation, bands and reliefs, and the Welsh tax has no equivalent of the English first time buyer relief.

front: What features do the two land transaction taxes share, and how should you deal with reliefs in an attendance note?
back: Both are payable by the buyer, both are calculated on a slice basis so each portion of the price is taxed at the rate for its band, both carry higher rates for additional residential properties and corporate purchases, and both require a return and payment within a short statutory period after the effective date. Say which tax applies and why, whether a relief such as group relief or charities relief is in point and on what conditions, and that you will compute the figure from the rates given in the materials.

front: What must you establish from the lease when acting for a buyer of a flat?
back: Read the lease and establish the unexpired term, the ground rent and any review, the service charge and any restriction on what the client actually wants to do. The tenant typically repairs the interior while the landlord repairs the structure, exterior and common parts through the service charge, so check the covenants dovetail and check the apportionment, the reserve fund, arrears and any planned major works.

front: Distinguish an absolute and a qualified alienation covenant, and explain forfeiture.
back: An absolute covenant prohibits assignment outright. A qualified covenant requires the landlord's consent, and statute implies that consent is not to be unreasonably withheld and imposes a duty to respond within a reasonable time. Forfeiture is the landlord's remedy for breach under a forfeiture clause; a lender will insist on notice before proceedings, and a mortgagee or tenant may apply for relief from forfeiture.

front: When does a business tenancy have security of tenure, and what does a section 25 notice do?
back: A business tenancy has security of tenure under Part II of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 unless the parties contracted out using the statutory notice and declaration procedure before the lease was granted. A protected tenancy continues until ended in a statutory way. The landlord ends or renews it by serving a section 25 notice, giving between six and twelve months' notice and stating whether renewal is opposed and on which statutory ground.

front: How is the legal estate held where two or more people buy together, and what varies?
back: The legal estate is always held on a joint tenancy on trust, with no more than four legal owners. What varies is the equitable interest. Joint tenants in equity own the whole together and survivorship applies, so the survivor takes automatically whatever the will says. Tenants in common own distinct shares which pass under the will or on intestacy, and the register carries a form A restriction.

front: How can an equitable joint tenancy be severed, and what is the result?
back: By written notice to the other joint tenants, by an act operating on a share, by mutual agreement, or by a course of dealing. Severance converts the severing owner's interest into a tenancy in common of a share equal to one divided by the number of joint tenants, so with two owners each takes a half, and any remaining joint tenants stay joint tenants of the balance. Survivorship no longer applies to the severed share.

front: What co ownership questions belong in a purchase interview, and when can you not act for both buyers?
back: Ask what each is contributing, whether either has children from a previous relationship, and what each wants to happen on death. Unequal contributions or a wish to leave a share elsewhere point to a tenancy in common with a declaration of trust recording the shares. Where the interests of two co buyers actually conflict, or one appears to be under pressure, you cannot simply act for both, and a partner providing money but taking no legal interest should take independent advice.

front: What must a solicitor acting for both buyer and lender do before the advance is released?
back: Check the title is good and marketable, comply with the lender's handbook instructions, and give a certificate of title. Acting for both is permitted where the mortgage is a standard one.

front: Give examples of matters that must be reported to the lender.
back: A price differing from that stated in the mortgage offer, a direct payment between seller and buyer, an occupier who is not a borrower, and a recent transaction at an undervalue. Each affects the lender's security or its lending decision.

front: A buyer tells you a relative is secretly funding part of the price and expects a share. What do you do?
back: Your duty of disclosure to each client pulls in opposite directions, so you cannot keep the information from the lender and continue to act for both. Explain that you must report it. If the client refuses consent you must cease to act for one or both.

front: What does customer due diligence require, and when is enhanced due diligence needed?
back: Identify the client, verify that identity from a reliable independent source, identify any beneficial owner where the client is a company or trust, and understand the purpose and intended nature of the transaction. Enhanced due diligence applies where risk is higher, for example a politically exposed person or a high risk third country. Due diligence is ongoing, not a box ticked once at the start.

front: Distinguish source of funds from source of wealth.
back: Source of funds asks where the money for this particular purchase comes from, evidenced by bank statements showing accumulation, a mortgage offer, a gift letter or a completion statement from a related sale. Source of wealth asks how the client came by their wealth overall, whether from employment, a business sale, inheritance or investment. A statement showing a large recent unexplained credit shows funds without wealth, and that is not enough.

front: Name the money laundering red flags worth spotting in a conveyancing file.
back: An unexplained third party paying all or part of the price, a rushed cash purchase with no lender doing its own checks, a price obviously out of line with value in either direction, a client indifferent to the property or the contract terms, and a request for funds to be returned to a different account or a third party. A transaction aborted after the money arrives, with a request for repayment elsewhere, is a classic laundering method.

front: You suspect the purchase money is criminal property. What must you do, and what must you not say?
back: Make an internal report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer, who decides whether to report to the National Crime Agency and, where consent is needed, to seek a defence against money laundering. Do not decide for yourself that the suspicion is unfounded, do not investigate the client, and do not complete until the position is resolved. Once a report has been or is being made it is an offence to disclose anything likely to prejudice an investigation, so you may tell the client neutrally that you cannot proceed at present but must not hint at the report.

front: State the test of testamentary capacity in Banks v Goodfellow.
back: The testator must understand the nature of the act of making a will and its effects, understand the extent of the property being disposed of, and comprehend and appreciate the claims to which they ought to give effect. No disorder of the mind may poison their affections or pervert their sense of right. Capacity is judged at the time of execution.

front: How does Parker v Felgate qualify the rule that capacity is judged at execution?
back: A will can stand where the testator had capacity when giving the instructions and, at execution, understood only that they were signing a will prepared in accordance with those instructions. It rescues a will where the testator has declined between instructions and signature.

front: Why does it matter that capacity is decision specific?
back: A client may lack capacity to manage an investment portfolio and still have capacity to make a simple will. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 supplies the framework, with a presumption of capacity and the rule that an unwise decision is not itself evidence of incapacity. Both points matter when a relative presses you to refuse instructions.

front: What is the golden rule, and what is its status?
back: It is prudent practice, not law. Where the testator is elderly, seriously ill or has had an episode of confusion, the will should be witnessed or approved by a medical practitioner who has satisfied themselves of capacity and recorded their reasoning, not merely signed. Failure to follow it does not by itself invalidate the will, but it invites dispute, and if the doctor declines you should record that too.

front: When does the presumption of knowledge and approval fall away?
back: Knowledge and approval is presumed on due execution by a testator with capacity. The presumption falls away where the circumstances excite suspicion, most commonly where there is a substantial gift to the person who arranged the will or gave the instructions.

front: What must be proved to establish undue influence in a will, and how do you protect against an allegation?
back: Undue influence here means coercion, not persuasion or appeals to affection. There is no presumption of undue influence in wills, so the person alleging it must prove the testator's will was overborne, although frailty and dependency make coercion easier to establish. Your protection is a contemporaneous file note of who was present, what the client said, and why they wish to benefit that person.

front: A daughter brings her mother to a will appointment and wants to sit in. How do you handle it, and what must you ask about?
back: Explain politely that you always see a client on their own for part of the appointment, because the will must record the client's own decisions. Take instructions in the client's own words and ask about the family before the gifts. Ask expressly about children from earlier relationships, cohabitants, stepchildren and anyone the client supports financially, since those are the people who bring 1975 Act claims.

front: Set out the formal requirements for a valid will under section 9 of the Wills Act 1837.
back: The will must be in writing and signed by the testator, or by another person in the testator's presence and by their direction, with the intention by that signature to give effect to the will. The signature must be made or acknowledged before two or more witnesses present at the same time. Each witness must then attest and sign, or acknowledge their signature, in the presence of the testator.

front: Must the witnesses be present for each other's signatures or know the contents of the will, and why include an attestation clause?
back: No on both counts. The witnesses need not be present when the other signs and need not know what the document says. An attestation clause reciting compliance with the formalities raises a presumption of due execution, so always include one.

front: What is the effect of section 15 of the Wills Act 1837 where a beneficiary witnesses the will?
back: A gift to an attesting witness, or to the spouse or civil partner of one, is void. The will and the attestation remain valid and only the gift fails, falling into residue. If two other valid witnesses also signed, the beneficiary witness may be disregarded and the gift saved.

front: In what four ways can a will be revoked?
back: By a later will or codicil revoking it expressly or by inconsistency. By a written declaration of revocation executed with the same formalities as a will. By burning, tearing or otherwise destroying it, by the testator or by another in their presence and by their direction and with intent to revoke, symbolic destruction being insufficient. And by marriage or civil partnership.

front: What is the effect of marriage on an existing will?
back: Marriage or the formation of a civil partnership revokes an earlier will, unless the will was expressly made in expectation of that particular marriage or civil partnership. Clients rarely realise this, so it should be raised whenever a client mentions an engagement.

front: What is the effect of divorce or dissolution on a will?
back: It does not revoke the will, although clients routinely assume it does. Under section 18A the former spouse or civil partner is treated as having died on the date the order was made final, so a gift to them lapses and their appointment as executor fails. The rest of the will stands.

front: Are unattested alterations to a signed will effective?
back: They are presumed to have been made after execution and are ineffective, unless the original wording is no longer apparent, or the alteration is itself executed with the section 9 formalities, usually by initialling in the margin. Never let a client amend a signed will with a pen.

front: When should you use a codicil and when a fresh will?
back: A codicil must be executed with the same formalities as a will, and it republishes the will as at the codicil's own date, which can revive gifts and alter a class gift. Use a codicil only for a small change, and prefer a fresh will where the changes are substantial.

front: Classify the types of gift in a will.
back: A specific gift is a particular identified item, such as a named grandfather clock. A general legacy is not tied to a particular asset, so the personal representatives must buy it in if the estate does not hold it. A pecuniary legacy is money, and a demonstrative legacy is money to be paid out of a named fund. Residue is what is left after debts, expenses, tax and legacies.

front: What happens if a will fails to dispose of the whole of residue?
back: The undisposed part passes on a partial intestacy, so it is distributed under the intestacy rules rather than under the will. Every will must contain a complete residuary gift, ideally with a substitutional and ultimate gift over.

front: What is ademption and how do you draft around it?
back: Ademption defeats a specific gift where the asset has ceased to exist or has been disposed of before death. A gift of a car identified by its registration number adeems if the client sells it. Draft instead by reference to whatever the client owns at death, for example any car I own at my death.

front: What is lapse, and how far does section 33 of the Wills Act 1837 help?
back: Lapse defeats a gift where the beneficiary dies before the testator, and the gift falls into residue. Section 33 substitutes the issue of the testator's children or remoter issue who predecease leaving issue alive at the death, unless the will shows a contrary intention. It does not apply to nephews, nieces, friends or siblings, so draft an express substitution clause rather than relying on it.

front: Why do the class closing rules matter when drafting a class gift?
back: A class gift such as one to such of my grandchildren as survive me closes once a member takes a vested interest, so a grandchild born later can be excluded. Say expressly in the will when the class is to close so the client's intention governs rather than the default rule.

front: What does a survivorship clause achieve, and what happens where the order of deaths is uncertain?
back: A clause requiring survival for a stated period, commonly 28 or 30 days, stops an estate passing twice on a common accident. Where the order of deaths is uncertain, section 184 of the Law of Property Act 1925 presumes the elder died first, subject to the modification that applies to spouses on intestacy.

front: Who takes on intestacy where the deceased leaves a spouse or civil partner but no issue?
back: The surviving spouse or civil partner takes the whole estate, and no other relative takes anything. The estate passes under sections 46 and 47 of the Administration of Estates Act 1925.

front: How is an intestate estate shared where there is a spouse and issue?
back: The spouse takes the personal chattels absolutely, a statutory legacy free of tax and costs with interest from death, and half the balance of residue absolutely. The other half of the balance goes to the issue on the statutory trusts. The statutory legacy is a fixed sum set by order and uprated periodically, so never guess it; it will be given to you. The spouse must survive by 28 days to take, and a judicially separated or former spouse takes nothing.

front: Where there is no surviving spouse, in what order do relatives take on intestacy?
back: The estate goes to the first category producing a living taker, in this order: issue, then parents, then brothers and sisters of the whole blood, then brothers and sisters of the half blood, then grandparents, then uncles and aunts of the whole blood, then uncles and aunts of the half blood. If none survives, the estate passes to the Crown as bona vacantia.

front: How do the statutory trusts work, and who is excluded?
back: Beneficiaries take in equal shares contingently on reaching 18 or marrying or forming a civil partnership earlier, with the issue of a predeceased member taking their parent's share per stirpes. Adopted children count as children of the adopters. Stepchildren do not unless adopted, and a cohabitant takes nothing on intestacy however long the relationship.

front: What right does a surviving spouse have over the family home on intestacy?
back: The spouse may require the family home to be appropriated towards their entitlement under the Intestates' Estates Act 1952. It is a right to have the house set against their share, not a right to extra value.

front: Who may apply under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975?
back: The spouse or civil partner; a former spouse or civil partner who has not remarried; a cohabitant who lived with the deceased as spouse or civil partner in the same household throughout the two years before death; a child of the deceased; a person treated as a child of the family; and any person maintained wholly or partly by the deceased immediately before death.

front: What are the two standards of provision under the 1975 Act?
back: The surviving spouse standard is such provision as is reasonable in all the circumstances, whether or not required for maintenance. Every other category of applicant is limited to what is reasonable for their maintenance.

front: What factors does the court weigh on a 1975 Act claim?
back: The section 3 factors: the applicant's present and future resources and needs, those of other applicants and of the beneficiaries, the obligations the deceased had, the size and nature of the estate, any disability, and any other relevant matter including conduct.

front: What is the time limit for a 1975 Act claim, and what does it mean for the personal representatives?
back: A claim must be brought within six months of the grant, extendable only with the court's permission. Personal representatives should consider waiting out that six month period before distributing, and the deadline belongs in your attendance note.

front: How does an executor's authority differ from an administrator's?
back: An executor is appointed by the will and their authority runs from the date of death, so acts before the grant are valid and probate merely confirms the title. An administrator is appointed by the court and has no authority at all until letters of administration issue.

front: Name the three types of grant and when each issues.
back: A grant of probate issues where a valid will appoints a proving executor. Letters of administration with the will annexed issue where there is a valid will but no executor able and willing to act, entitlement following rule 20 of the Non Contentious Probate Rules 1987. Simple letters of administration issue on intestacy under the rule 22 order, which tracks the intestacy order of entitlement.

front: How many personal representatives may take a grant, and when are two required?
back: No grant may issue to more than four personal representatives. Where a minority interest or a life interest arises, at least two administrators or a trust corporation will normally be required, so that a good receipt can be given for capital money.

front: Explain the chain of representation and its limits.
back: It applies to executors only. Where a sole or last surviving proving executor dies, their own executor becomes executor of the original estate automatically once probate of their will is granted. The chain is broken by intestacy or by a failure to prove. Administrators have no chain, so a grant de bonis non is needed.

front: Set out the route of an administration from death up to the grant.
back: Register the death and obtain certified copies of the certificate, locate the will and check its execution, then notify asset holders and obtain date of death valuations of every asset and liability, including joint property, pensions, policies and lifetime gifts in the previous seven years. Decide whether an inheritance tax account is needed or the estate is excepted, and pay the tax due on delivery, using the direct payment scheme or a loan if necessary. Then apply for the grant with the statement of truth.

front: What must personal representatives do after the grant, up to distribution?
back: Collect the assets and pay the funeral, testamentary expenses and debts in the statutory order. Advertise under section 27 of the Trustee Act 1925 to protect against unknown claimants. Then pay the legacies, obtain receipts, and prepare estate accounts of capital, income and distribution for the residuary beneficiaries to approve.

front: Describe the structure of inheritance tax on death, without figures.
back: Inheritance tax is charged on the value transferred on death and on chargeable lifetime transfers. Each estate has a nil rate band taxed at nil per cent, with the excess taxed at the death rate. A residence nil rate band is available in addition where a qualifying residential interest is closely inherited by lineal descendants, tapered away above a stated estate value, with a downsizing addition where the home was sold or downsized. The rates and thresholds are given in the assessment materials.

front: How is an unused nil rate band transferred, and which transfers are exempt?
back: Any unused proportion of a deceased spouse's or civil partner's nil rate band and residence nil rate band is transferable to the survivor, on a claim. Transfers between spouses and civil partners are exempt, subject to a cap where the transferee is not long term UK resident. Gifts to charity are exempt, and a reduced death rate applies where a stated proportion of the net estate passes to charity.

front: What do business relief and agricultural relief do, and what are their conditions?
back: They reduce the value transferred on qualifying business and agricultural property, subject to minimum ownership periods and to the exclusion of businesses wholly or mainly dealing in investments. From 6 April 2026 the reliefs run through a capped allowance, with full relief up to a stated allowance and a lower rate above it. The allowance and the relief rates will be supplied in the materials.

front: How are lifetime gifts to individuals treated, and what is taper relief?
back: They are potentially exempt transfers and drop out of account entirely if the donor survives seven years. If the donor dies within seven years the gift becomes chargeable, using the nil rate band first. Taper relief then reduces the tax, not the value, on a sliding scale once the donor has survived at least three years. Gifts into most trusts are immediately chargeable instead.

front: What is a reservation of benefit, and which lifetime exemptions should you look for?
back: A reservation of benefit arises where the client gives an asset away but continues to enjoy it, for example giving away the house and going on living in it, so the asset is still treated as part of the estate. Look also for the annual exemption, small gifts, gifts in consideration of marriage and normal expenditure out of income. The monetary limits will be given to you.

front: Which trusts essentials arise inside a probate file, and what does a trustee owe?
back: An express trust needs the three certainties from Knight v Knight: intention, subject matter and objects. A bare trust holds property for an adult absolutely entitled, who can call for it under Saunders v Vautier, while a life interest gives the life tenant the income and the remainderman the capital, so trustees must hold an even hand. Under a discretionary trust the trustees select among a class, so no beneficiary has more than a hope until an appointment is made. Trustees owe a duty of care under section 1 of the Trustee Act 2000, must have regard to the standard investment criteria and take proper advice, and must not profit from the trust or act in a position of conflict.

front: What are the features of trading as a sole trader?
back: The trader carries on business personally, so there is no separate legal person and no registration. Liability is unlimited. Profits are taxed as trading income under income tax with national insurance, and finance comes only from personal resources and borrowing.
