front: When does a general partnership arise, and what liability do the partners have?
back: Under the Partnership Act 1890 a partnership arises where two or more persons carry on a business in common with a view of profit. It needs no writing or formality, so it can arise by accident, which is a favourite examiner trap. Liability is unlimited, joint for debts and joint and several for wrongs, and partners are taxed individually on their profit share.

front: Why do professional firms use a limited liability partnership?
back: An LLP is incorporated under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 and is a body corporate, so it contracts in its own name, members' liability is limited and it files accounts publicly. Members are nonetheless taxed transparently, as if they were partners. The entity owes the debts and members are agents of it rather than of each other, so a members' agreement is vital.

front: What does a private company limited by shares offer, and at what cost?
back: It has separate legal personality, limits members' liability to any amount unpaid on their shares, pays corporation tax on its own profits, and can raise money by issuing shares as well as borrowing. Its affairs are public and the cost is formality: statutory registers, formal decision making and real directors' duties. Weigh liability, tax, formality and finance together in every case.

front: What is the status of the certificate of incorporation and of the model articles?
back: The certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the company exists. Without bespoke articles the Model Articles for private companies limited by shares apply, and they apply anyway so far as not excluded or modified. The articles bind the company and its members as if signed by each of them, but only as to membership rights, and are amended by special resolution.

front: Why should a minority shareholder's veto sit in the shareholders' agreement rather than the articles?
back: The articles are public, bind all members present and future, and can be changed on a seventy five per cent majority, so a right sitting only in the articles can be voted away by the very majority the veto exists to control. A shareholders' agreement is a private contract binding only its parties and can be varied only by their unanimous consent.

front: How is a director removed under section 168 of the Companies Act 2006?
back: By ordinary resolution, but special notice of twenty eight days is required, the director may make written representations and be heard, and a written resolution cannot be used, so a general meeting must be held. Appointments and terminations are notified to Companies House.

front: List the general duties of a director codified in sections 171 to 177.
back: Act within powers; promote the success of the company for the benefit of the members as a whole, having regard to the listed factors; exercise independent judgment; exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence on a test both objective and subjective; avoid conflicts of interest; not accept benefits from third parties; and declare an interest in a proposed transaction.

front: How and when must a director declare an interest in a transaction?
back: An interest in a proposed transaction must be declared to the other directors under section 177 before the company enters into it. An interest in a transaction the company has already entered into must be declared under section 182.

front: What is a substantial property transaction and what approval does it need?
back: An acquisition or disposal of a non cash asset between the company and a director or a person connected with a director, where the value of the asset exceeds the statutory percentage of the company's asset value or the statutory ceiling. It requires an ordinary resolution of the members. The monetary limits will be given to you.

front: What is required before a company lends to one of its directors?
back: Approval by ordinary resolution of the members, supported by a memorandum setting out the nature of the loan, its amount and its purpose. Exceptions apply, including small loans and expenditure on company business.

front: How is a breach of duty by a director remedied, and can the members forgive it?
back: Breach is remedied as the underlying equitable or common law rule would be: rescission, recovery of property, an account of profits, equitable compensation or damages. A transaction made without a required approval is voidable, and the director and any connected person must account for gains and indemnify the company. Members may ratify by ordinary resolution, but votes cast in favour by the director in breach and by any member connected with him are disregarded.

front: State the majorities for ordinary and special resolutions, and give examples of each.
back: An ordinary resolution needs more than fifty per cent of the votes cast; a special resolution needs not less than seventy five per cent. Altering the articles, disapplying pre emption rights and voluntary winding up need a special resolution. Appointing and removing directors, and approving substantial property transactions and director loans, need an ordinary resolution.

front: How does a written resolution work in a private company, and what cannot be done by one?
back: Almost any resolution may be passed as a written resolution circulated to every eligible member. The threshold is measured against the total voting rights of all eligible members, not those who reply, so silence counts as opposition. Removal of a director and removal of an auditor cannot be done this way and need a meeting.

front: What notice is required for a general meeting, and how can members force one?
back: Notice is fourteen clear days. Short notice requires the consent of a majority in number of the members holding ninety per cent of the voting shares. Members holding five per cent of the voting capital may require a meeting to be held.

front: What must a petitioner show under section 994, and what is the usual remedy?
back: That the company's affairs are being conducted in a manner unfairly prejudicial to the interests of the members generally or of some part of them. Both unfairness and prejudice are needed, judged against the bargain the members actually made. The usual remedy is an order that the majority buy the petitioner's shares.

front: How does a derivative claim differ from an unfair prejudice petition?
back: In a derivative claim a member sues on behalf of the company for a wrong done to the company by a director. The court's permission is required to continue the claim, and any remedy belongs to the company rather than to the member.

front: When may directors of a private company allot shares without a members' resolution?
back: Where the company has only one class of shares, the directors may allot without further authority unless the articles say otherwise. In any other case they need authority given by ordinary resolution or in the articles.

front: What do the statutory pre emption rights require, and how are they removed?
back: Equity securities allotted for cash must first be offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their existing holdings. The rights can be disapplied by special resolution. They protect a shareholder against dilution, so check them before any share issue to a new investor.

front: How are shares in a private company transferred, and when is the transferee a member?
back: By stock transfer form delivered with the share certificate. The transfer binds the company only on registration of the transferee in the register of members, so the register, not the form, determines membership.

front: Out of what may a dividend lawfully be paid, and who declares it?
back: Only out of profits available for distribution, meaning accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses, judged by reference to the relevant accounts. A final dividend is declared by ordinary resolution on the board's recommendation. An interim dividend is paid by the board.

front: What are the consequences of an unlawful dividend?
back: A shareholder who knew or had reasonable grounds to believe the dividend was unlawful must repay it. The directors who authorised it may have to make good the loss to the company.

front: What default terms does the Partnership Act 1890 supply, and why do they rarely suit?
back: Profits and losses are shared equally whatever the capital contributed, with no salary and no interest on capital. Every partner may manage, ordinary matters are decided by majority but a change in the nature of the business needs unanimity, and no new partner may be admitted without unanimous consent. The firm dissolves on a partner's death or bankruptcy, or on notice where the partnership is at will, so a partner can otherwise dissolve the business by letter.

front: How far does one partner bind the firm, and how is liability shared?
back: Every partner is an agent of the firm, which is bound by an act done in the usual way of the firm's business unless the partner lacked authority and the third party knew it. Partners are liable jointly for debts incurred while they are partners, and jointly and severally for wrongful acts and misapplied money.

front: What liability does a retiring partner keep, and what steps reduce it?
back: The retiring partner remains liable for debts incurred before retirement unless released by novation. They also remain liable for later debts to anyone who dealt with the firm before and has not had notice of the retirement. Give actual notice to existing customers and publish notice in the London Gazette for everyone else.

front: What are the two tests of corporate insolvency?
back: The cash flow test, whether the company can pay its debts as they fall due. And the balance sheet test, whether the value of its assets is less than its liabilities, taking into account contingent and prospective liabilities.

front: What is the administrator's statutory hierarchy of objectives, and how is an administrator appointed?
back: Rescue the company as a going concern; failing that, achieve a better result for creditors as a whole than on a winding up; otherwise realise property to distribute to secured or preferential creditors. Appointment is by court order, or out of court by the company, the directors or a qualifying floating charge holder. A moratorium halts enforcement while the administration continues.

front: Distinguish the three forms of liquidation.
back: Compulsory liquidation follows a court order, typically on a creditor's petition. A creditors' voluntary liquidation is begun by the members but controlled by the creditors. A members' voluntary liquidation requires a statutory declaration of solvency, so it is used only where the company can pay its debts in full.

front: What is a transaction at an undervalue for clawback purposes?
back: A transaction where the company received no consideration, or significantly less consideration than it gave, entered into within two years before the onset of insolvency at a time when the company was unable to pay its debts. The office holder may apply to restore the position to what it would have been.

front: What must be shown to set aside a preference?
back: That the company did something putting a creditor, surety or guarantor in a better position than they would have been in on a liquidation, within six months before the onset of insolvency, or two years for a connected person, at a time when the company was unable to pay its debts or became unable to do so as a result, and that the company was influenced by a desire to prefer. That desire is presumed where the person preferred is connected with the company.

front: When does wrongful trading arise and what can the court order?
back: Where a director knew, or ought to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect of the company avoiding insolvent liquidation and the company nonetheless went into insolvent liquidation or administration. It is a defence for the director to show that from that point he took every step to minimise the potential loss to creditors that he ought to have taken. The court may order the director to contribute to the company's assets.

front: How does fraudulent trading differ from wrongful trading, and what is the disqualification exposure?
back: Fraudulent trading requires dishonesty: business carried on with intent to defraud creditors. Wrongful trading requires no dishonesty, only the objective and subjective standard of what the director knew or ought to have concluded. Either can lead to disqualification as a director for up to fifteen years.

front: What do you advise a director of a company on the brink of insolvency?
back: Meet as a board and minute the reasoning, take insolvency advice at once, and stop incurring credit that cannot be paid. Do not prefer one creditor over another and do not sell assets cheaply to a connected party. Shift the focus of decision making from the shareholders to the creditors.

front: State the general prohibition and the consequences of breaching it.
back: Under section 19 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, no person may carry on a regulated activity in the United Kingdom, or purport to do so, unless authorised or exempt. Breach is a criminal offence and can make the agreement unenforceable.

front: What are the limbs of a regulated activity, and which investments are specified?
back: A specified activity, carried on by way of business, relating to a specified investment. Specified investments include shares, debentures, government securities, units in collective investment schemes, options, futures, contracts of insurance and regulated mortgage contracts. Land, and the goodwill and assets of a business, are not, which is why an asset sale often raises no financial services issue while a share sale does. Specified activities include dealing as agent, arranging deals, managing investments and advising on the merits of a particular investment.

front: Name the exclusions that take an activity outside the financial services regime.
back: Acting as agent where the transaction is entered into on the advice of an authorised person, arrangements made with or through an authorised person, and activities carried on in administering an estate or a trust. There is also the takeover exclusion, for an acquisition of shares carrying a specified proportion of the voting power where the object is day to day control, which is why buying the whole share capital of a trading company often falls outside the regime.

front: What is the professional firms route, and in what order should you ask the financial services questions?
back: A solicitors' firm may rely on the Part 20 exemption for members of a designated professional body: the activity must be incidental to the professional services provided, the firm must account to the client for any commission, the activity must not be a prohibited one, and the firm must comply with the SRA Financial Services Scope Rules. Ask in order: is there a specified investment, is there a specified activity, is it by way of business, does an exclusion apply, and if not can the firm rely on the exemption. If it cannot, refer the client to an authorised person.

front: When must customer due diligence be applied on a corporate matter, and what does it involve?
back: Before establishing a business relationship or carrying out an occasional transaction. It means identifying the client and verifying identity from a reliable independent source, identifying any beneficial owner and taking reasonable measures to verify their identity, understanding the purpose and intended nature of the relationship, and monitoring throughout. Enhanced due diligence is required where risk is high, for example a party in a high risk third country, a politically exposed person or their family member or close associate, or an unusually large or complex transaction with no apparent economic purpose.

front: How do you identify the beneficial owner of a corporate client?
back: Verify the company's existence and constitution, then identify the individuals who ultimately own or control more than twenty five per cent of the shares or voting rights, or who otherwise exercise control. Check the register of people with significant control, and watch for ownership layered through offshore vehicles.

front: On a business sale, what do source of funds and source of wealth each ask, and what are the red flags?
back: Source of funds asks where the money for this transaction comes from and by what route. Source of wealth asks how the client came to have the wealth from which it is drawn. Both must be asked. Red flags include a price that does not match the value of the business, funds from a third party or an unconnected jurisdiction, late changes to the structure or the purchaser, reluctance to give ownership information, and an offer to pay in cash.

front: You suspect money laundering on a corporate transaction. What must you do, and what must you not say?
back: Report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer as soon as practicable where you know or suspect, or have reasonable grounds to suspect, that another person is engaged in money laundering. Failing to disclose in the regulated sector is itself an offence, and an authorised disclosure with consent may give a defence to a principal offence. Once a disclosure has been made, do not tell the client or anyone else about the report or a contemplated investigation where that is likely to prejudice it. Take the officer's advice, and if you cease to act give no reason.

front: Which SQE2 stations carry the ethics criterion, and which single station does not?
back: Every written station, the advocacy station and the attendance note carry the criterion to identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity. Only the client interview lacks it, because that station is marked by the assessor playing the client on skills alone. The ethics criterion sits in the application of law half, so missing it costs a whole criterion out of three.

front: What does it mean that ethics in SQE2 is never flagged, and what standard are you held to?
back: No station will tell you a conduct issue exists. The issue sits inside an ordinary looking client problem and you must see it, name it and deal with it honestly. The standard is that of a competent newly qualified solicitor: you are not asked to cite paragraph numbers, you are asked to notice, reason and act.

front: Which three parts of the SRA Standards and Regulations are examinable in SQE2?
back: The SRA Principles; the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, called in assessments the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors; and the SRA Code of Conduct for Firms, the last only in relation to managers in authorised firms and compliance officers.

front: List the seven SRA Principles.
back: Act in a way that upholds the constitutional principle of the rule of law and the proper administration of justice; in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the profession and in legal services provided by authorised persons; with independence; with honesty; with integrity; in a way that encourages equality, diversity and inclusion; and in the best interests of each client.

front: Two SRA Principles point in opposite directions on your facts. Which one wins?
back: Those Principles which safeguard the wider public interest take precedence over the individual client's interests: the rule of law and the proper administration of justice, and public confidence in a trustworthy solicitors' profession and a safe and effective market for regulated legal services. Where relevant you should tell the client of the circumstances in which your duty to the court and your other professional obligations will outweigh your duty to them. A candidate who resolves the clash by doing what the client wants has failed the criterion, however commercially attractive that answer looks.

front: What is the difference between honesty and integrity, and why does naming the right one earn marks?
back: Honesty is close to the lay meaning: not lying, not deceiving, not stealing. Integrity is wider, the moral soundness expected of a profession the public trusts. You can be technically honest and still lack integrity, by letting a client rest on a misapprehension you created or by turning a blind eye to obvious wrongdoing. Say which of the two is engaged and why.

front: What must a firm and its managers do under the SRA Code of Conduct for Firms?
back: A firm must have effective systems and controls, and managers are personally responsible for compliance within their area of management. The firm must appoint a compliance officer for legal practice (COLP) and a compliance officer for finance and administration (COFA), and serious breaches must be reported to the SRA promptly.

front: A client gives you a lawful instruction that you consider is against their own interests. What do you do?
back: Best interests are not the same as instructions. Advise the client why the instruction is against their interests, record the advice, and if they persist you may generally act on it. If the instruction is unlawful, or would put you in breach of your own duties, you cannot act on it.

front: What does the Principle of independence prohibit in practice?
back: It prohibits letting your professional judgment be directed by anyone else's interests: a client, a litigation funder, a referrer of work, or your own financial interest in the outcome. Independence is a separate Principle from best interests, and pressure from a paying referrer engages it directly.

front: How do the duty of confidentiality and the duty of disclosure differ, and which prevails?
back: You must keep the affairs of current and former clients confidential unless disclosure is required or permitted by law or the client consents. Separately, where you act for a client you must make them aware of all information material to their matter of which you have knowledge. Confidentiality is the stronger duty and prevails.

front: You hold confidential information about client A that is material to client B's matter. What can you do?
back: You do not disclose it. You either decline to act for B, or act only with informed consent and effective safeguards where the rules permit. The disclosure duty does not override the confidentiality owed to A, and A's confidentiality survives the end of the retainer.

front: Why is the duty not to mislead broader than a duty not to lie?
back: You must not mislead or attempt to mislead the court, your opponent or anyone else by your own acts or omissions, or by being complicit in your client's. Standing by while the court proceeds on a basis you know to be false is a breach, so silence can mislead just as effectively as a statement.

front: What is an own interest conflict, and is there any consent exception?
back: It is a conflict between your own interests, or your firm's, and the client's: the client complains of your negligence, wants to buy your house, or wants to leave you a legacy. There is no consent exception. If there is an own interest conflict, or a significant risk of one, you cannot act.

front: What is a client conflict, and what are the two narrow exceptions?
back: It is a conflict between duties owed to two or more current clients on the same or a related matter, and the general rule is that you cannot act. The exceptions are a substantially common interest, and clients competing for the same objective which only one can attain. Both require informed written consent from all clients, that it is reasonable to act, and effective safeguards.

front: Give an example of each client conflict exception, and one situation neither exception can save.
back: A substantially common interest covers two partners incorporating a company on agreed terms, sharing a clear common purpose and a strong consensus on how to achieve it. Competing for the same objective covers rival bidders at auction or in a tender. Neither saves acting for the seller and the buyer on the same conveyance, because they are opposed on price, condition and risk.

front: What must you tell a client about costs, and when?
back: Give the client information they can understand, including the best possible information on the likely overall cost, at the outset and as the matter goes on. If an estimate is going to be exceeded, tell the client before it is exceeded, not afterwards.

front: What must a client be told about complaints, and where does a complaint go?
back: Tell the client at the outset, in writing, about your complaints procedure and about their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman, including how and when. Deal with complaints promptly, fairly and free of charge, and if one is unresolved after eight weeks confirm that right again in writing. Service complaints go to the firm and then the Ombudsman; allegations of misconduct go to the SRA.

front: What counts as an undertaking, and does it have to be written or use the word undertake?
back: An undertaking is a statement by or for you or your firm, to someone who reasonably relies on it, that you or the firm will do something, cause it to be done, or refrain from something. It need not use the word undertake and need not be in writing, so an email or a sentence on the telephone can bind you.

front: The client withdraws instructions and never puts you in funds. What happens to an undertaking you have already given?
back: Nothing. It binds you personally, the court can enforce it against you, and it is not discharged because the client fails to put you in funds or withdraws instructions. That is why you undertake only what is within your own control.

front: How do you draft an undertaking safely?
back: Put it in writing and keep a copy; undertake only what is within your own control, never something depending on a third party or the client's cooperation; make it certain as to what, to whom, by when and on what condition; make it conditional on a verifiable event such as completion; never undertake to pay money you do not hold; record it centrally and confirm discharge in writing.

front: Which parts of Legal Services are examinable in SQE2, and in which practice areas?
back: Legal Services is not examined in SQE2 except for money laundering and financial services. The specification attaches money laundering to BOTH Property Practice and Business Law and Practice, and financial services to Business Law and Practice only. The Legal System of England and Wales, including constitutional, administrative and EU law, and Solicitors' Accounts are not examined at all.

front: What does client due diligence require, and when does enhanced due diligence apply?
back: Identify and verify the client and any beneficial owner, understand the purpose and intended nature of the relationship, and keep it under review. Enhanced due diligence applies in higher risk situations, such as a politically exposed person or a party connected with a high risk third country.

front: You suspect that funds in a property transaction are criminal property. What do you do, and what must you not do?
back: Do not deal with the property and report internally to the firm's money laundering reporting officer, who decides whether to report to the National Crime Agency. Do not tell the client what you have done or why, because tipping off is itself a criminal offence.

front: Name the money laundering red flags to watch for in a transaction.
back: Unexplained third party funding, cash, a rushed transaction with no commercial rationale, a price that does not match the property, evasiveness about the source of funds, and a late change of buyer or of banking details.

front: What is the financial services point you need in outline for Business Law and Practice?
back: Carrying on a regulated activity by way of business requires authorisation unless an exclusion applies, or unless the firm relies on the exemption for professional firms carrying on regulated activities incidental to professional services under Part 20 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. Arranging a share sale, or advising on the merits of an investment, is the trigger to notice.

front: When does a non-disclosure agreement become improper under the SRA warning notice?
back: An NDA is lawful and common, but becomes improper when used to prevent proper disclosure or to intimidate. Warning markers are a clause purporting to stop the person reporting a criminal offence to the police, cooperating with an investigation, making a protected disclosure to a regulator, or seeking medical or legal advice, and a clause requiring them to state something untrue such as that no complaint was made.

front: A partner asks you to send a settlement offer to a former employee with a 48 hour deadline, no chance to take advice, and a clause saying she may tell nobody about anything. How do you deal with it?
back: Advise that clauses preventing protected disclosure or reporting should not be included, record that advice, allow a proper opportunity for her to take independent legal advice, and carve out the permitted disclosures expressly in the agreement itself. Pressure, threatening language and a very short deadline on an unrepresented person are themselves warning markers. If the client insists on the improper clause, you do not draft it.

front: What is a SLAPP, and what are its markers?
back: A strategic lawsuit against public participation is litigation, or the threat of it, used to silence, intimidate or exhaust someone publishing on a matter of public interest, rather than to vindicate a genuine right. Markers include a target who is a journalist, campaigner, whistleblower or academic, a weak or exaggerated claim that never identifies what is actually false, aggressive correspondence in tone and volume, a very short deadline, a blanket not for publication label, threats of ruinous costs, and suing the individual as well as the publisher.

front: A client wants a robust letter before action against a journalist. Where is the line between vigorous advocacy and a SLAPP?
back: You may pursue a genuine claim vigorously, but you may not use the process to intimidate. If the aim is to suppress rather than to remedy, advise the client against it and decline to send the correspondence. A technically accomplished improper letter is worse than a clumsy one, because it is more effective.

front: What are the six steps of the repeatable method for an unflagged ethics issue?
back: Notice the trigger; name the duty engaged in plain words; identify who the duty is owed to; weigh the competing duties using the tie breaker of the public interest in the proper administration of justice and the rule of law; decide and state what you will and will not do; and record it in an attendance note, a confirming letter, and a report to the supervisor or COLP where required.

front: Which step of the six step ethics method do candidates skip, and why does it decide the outcome?
back: Step three, identifying who the duty is owed to: the client, the court, a third party, the profession or the regulator. Naming the person owed the duty is what shows whether confidentiality to a client or the duty not to mislead the court prevails, so skipping it leaves the weighing step with nothing to weigh.

front: Your buyer client says his uncle abroad, whom you have never met, will wire the deposit, and asks you not to mention it to the lender because it complicates things. What do you do?
back: The trigger is third party funds plus a request for concealment, engaging due diligence and source of funds and, because you also act for the lender, the duty not to mislead it and to pass on what is material to the offer. Verify the uncle and the source of funds, tell the client the lender must be informed and that you cannot proceed otherwise, cease to act if he refuses, and consider an internal report without tipping him off. Record it in a file note and a confirming letter.

front: A client charged with theft tells you she took the goods knowing they were not hers, then says she will plead not guilty and give evidence that she thought she had paid. What can and cannot you do?
back: Confidentiality survives and stops you telling anyone what she said, but you cannot mislead the court. Advise her she may plead not guilty and put the prosecution to proof, but that you cannot call her to give an account you know to be untrue. If she insists you must cease to act, and you may not tell the court why. Record the confession and the advice in a full attendance note.

front: An elderly client attends with her nephew, who does most of the talking. She wants to leave the residue to him and five thousand pounds to you for your kindness. What do you do?
back: The issues are an own interest conflict, independence, integrity, capacity, and knowledge and approval. See her alone, satisfy yourself as to capacity and consider a medical opinion, and do not prepare a will conferring a significant benefit on you: given the size of the gift, decline and refer her elsewhere. Record who was present and what was said in a full attendance note.

front: A single director of a company instructs you in a Business Law matter. Who is your client, and what should you watch for?
back: Usually the company, not the individual, and their interests may diverge. Watch for conflicts between the company and its shareholders, for instructions that serve the director personally rather than the company, and for financial services issues on a share sale.

front: Name the recurring conduct traps in Dispute Resolution and in Property Practice.
back: In Dispute Resolution: misleading the other side, including by silence once an earlier statement has become untrue, and improper threats such as threatening criminal proceedings to gain advantage in a civil claim. In Property: money laundering red flags, acting for buyer and lender where a conflict may arise and material information must reach the lender, and acting for both seller and buyer.

front: Where can negotiation be assessed in SQE2, and where can it never appear?
back: There is no separate negotiation assessment, but every delivery contains at least one assessment involving negotiation. It can appear in the client interview and attendance note, in case and matter analysis, or in legal writing. It never appears in advocacy, legal research or legal drafting.

front: What is the difference between a position and an interest in a negotiation, and how does a strong answer use it?
back: A position is what a party says they want, for example ninety thousand pounds. An interest is why they want it: cash flow before a quarter day, vindication, or continuity of supply. Positions collide, but interests can be traded, so a strong answer identifies your client's interests and the other side's likely interests and proposes terms satisfying both, such as staged payments, a reference, a continued contract or an apology.

front: What is the BATNA, and how does it relate to the opening, target and reserve?
back: The best alternative to a negotiated agreement is what your client will do if no deal is struck, and it is the true measure of negotiating strength, so assess it first. The opening is the first offer, ambitious but justifiable; the target is the realistic outcome; the reserve or walk away point is the least favourable outcome the client will accept, set by reference to the BATNA and agreed with the client before the negotiation begins, not during it.

front: In a negotiation, what may you not say, and what are you not obliged to disclose?
back: You must not make a false statement of fact to your opponent, the court or anyone else, must not let your client make one through you, must correct a statement that was true when made but has since become false, and must not take unfair advantage of an unrepresented opponent. You are not obliged to volunteer your client's reserve position, commercial motives or weaknesses. Saying my client is not prepared to go above eighty thousand pounds today is legitimate positioning; saying my client has no funds beyond eighty thousand pounds, when you know they do, is a false statement of fact and a breach.

front: You are asked to investigate an unregistered title. What are you given, and what are you looking for?
back: You are given an epitome of title, a schedule of the documents with copies attached, rather than an office copy of a register. You look for a good root of title, a document at least fifteen years old that deals with the whole legal and equitable estate, identifies the property clearly and casts no doubt on the title. From that root you trace an unbroken chain of ownership to the seller, and you search the Land Charges Department against the name of every estate owner revealed, because in unregistered land incumbrances are registered against names and not against the property.
